We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

title: Joint Movable Antenna Positioning and Precoding for ISAC via a Two-Timescale Model-Based GNN
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Movable antennas (MAs) allow an integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) base station (BS) to reshape multiuser channels and angular sensitivity. For monostatic multiuser communication and multi-target elevation and azimuth estimation, we minimize the expected target-averaged angular Bayesian Cramér-Rao bound (BCRB) subject to per-user block-level and long-term rate requirements. To avoid repeated online optimization, we propose a two-timescale model-based graph neural network (TT-MBGNN) over antennas, users, and targets. The slow policy selects positions from long-term statistics to reduce movement overhead, while the fast policy learns complex corrections to a regularized zero-forcing (RZF) reference using post-movement channels and target-angle priors. We jointly train both policies through a differentiable model of rates and BCRB, without optimization-generated labels. Across tested rate requirements, the network yields lower sensing bounds than variants using a fixed array, RZF, or both, with any-user fast-rate violations in 0.31-2.63% of test blocks. Frozen policies provide competitive sensing bounds for unseen user and target counts, and ten fine-tuning epochs improve communication reliability at higher user counts. Across tested network sizes, our framework achieves up to 3 dB lower BCRB than an idealized alternating-optimization benchmark that uses known target reflection coefficients. The network computes precoders approximately 50-fold faster in matched batch-one tests.

title: Local asymptotic normality for Cox-Ingersoll-Ross drift parameters under high-frequency sampling and the strict Feller condition
summary: For the ergodic Cox--Ingersoll--Ross (CIR) diffusion with known diffusion scale and a fixed initial value, we prove local asymptotic normality (LAN) of the exactly sampled experiment for the drift parameters whenever the Feller index exceeds $1$, assuming only a vanishing mesh and a diverging observation horizon. This improves the previously known condition that the index exceed $(11+\sqrt{89})/2$. The proof cuts off the continuous score near $0$, recovers the remainder by exact conditional centering on each sampling interval, and transfers LAN by a conditional-likelihood argument.

title: A Unified Control Framework, Mathematical Model, and Five-layer Closed-loop Case Study for Embodied Intelligence Control Systems
summary: Embodied intelligence holds that an agent develops cognition and behavior through real-time body-environment interaction, so its control system must tightly couple perception, decision making, learning, optimization, constraints, and physical execution. This report asks whether a unified framework exists, how its mathematical models unify, and how the framework is realized computably. Four conclusions emerge. (1) No single framework is accepted, but the field converges on a common skeleton: from operational-space and whole-body control to MPC, reinforcement learning, active inference, and diffusion/flow policies, all reduce to constrained sequential decision making on the configuration manifold. (2) Two languages describe it-deterministic optimal control (Euler-Lagrange plus constrained OCP, reduced in real time to a QP) and probabilistic inference (MDP/POMDP plus free-energy minimization)-rigorously bridged by control as inference and KL/path-integral control. (3) Engineering unification is already achieved by constrained optimization; the new frontier is cross-morphology, cross-task shared representation. (4) The hardest gap is provable stability and safety, the entry point for spectral, geometric, differentiable-optimization, and safe-learning methods. A single-link manipulator then runs through all five layers: L4 parses the instruction into a reference, L3 identifies a Koopman lifted linear world model, L2 solves a receding constrained QP, L1 adds torque saturation and a CBF, and L0 is the true nonlinear plant. Closed-loop tracking RMSE is 0.0218 rad with all constraints satisfied and a world-model error near 5 x 10^-6 rad, reported with curves and a 3D animation.

title: Computing rare events in Lévy-driven systems via optimal control
summary: We extend the optimal control formulation of sample path large deviation theory, which has proven effective for numerical computation of instantons and sharp probability estimates in stochastic differential equations with Gaussian noise, to systems with light-tailed Lévy noise. In the scaling limit of small jumps and high intensity, such systems satisfy a large deviation principle of Freidlin-Wentzell type, with a running cost given by the Legendre transform of the noise cumulant generating function. We propose to numerically minimize this cost over noise realizations subject to the system dynamics, which yields the instanton without having to solve Hamilton's equations, and naturally handles degenerate and multiplicative noise. When the cumulant generating function has a bounded domain, the cost grows only linearly for large noise, and instantons can contain jumps. We analyze when jumps are not only admissible but optimal, depending on the subleading behavior of the cost and on the drift, and show how jumps can be resolved numerically through a time reparameterization that freezes physical time. For continuous instantons, we derive Riccati and Fredholm determinant expressions for the leading-order prefactor, and we discuss the modifications needed when the instanton jumps. We illustrate and validate our methods against Monte Carlo simulations in several examples: a two-dimensional nonlinear model, an active run-and-tumble particle with non-Gaussian tumbling noise, and the Ghil-Sellers energy balance climate model with Lévy-perturbed solar forcing.

title: Zero-shot diffusion image compression with sectioned codebooks and one channel code
summary: Zero-shot diffusion codecs such as Turbo-DDCM compress images without any training. In each coded step, the encoder selects noise vectors from one codebook and transmits a single index for the selected set. We propose sectioned codebooks. A coded step is divided into sections, and each section has its own large codebook and transmits its best vector as a short field of bits. A model based on order statistics quantifies how well the bits of a step are used and predicts the gain of sectioned codebooks from measurements of Turbo-DDCM alone. Fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms make sections of $2^{20}$ vectors practical. At equal bits, sectioned codebooks improve the PSNR of Turbo-DDCM by 0.18 to 0.51 dB on three datasets, improve LPIPS and DISTS, and save 16 to 21% of the bits at equal PSNR. Codecs that are robust to channel errors by design are usually compared only with unprotected codecs. We compare them, at equal total bits, with a codec protected by one channel code. With one BCH code, the sectioned codec outperforms all reported results of Robust Turbo-DDCM and BitFlat on two datasets, by up to 7.74 dB at the highest bit error rate. At the lowest bit error rate its margin over BitFlat is only 0.08 to 0.16 dB. When the code fails, the receiver can still decode the fields as received. Additional experiments cover burst errors and packet loss, and all observed gains of robust codecs stay within a limit derived from the channel capacity.

title: Asymptotic Divergence-Based Monitoring for Data Drift in Production AI Systems: A Discrete Case Approach
summary: We develop a complete asymptotic theory for monitoring data drift in production artificial intelligence (AI) systems whose inputs take values in a finite set of categories. The framework combines two complementary inferential tools. Under the no-drift hypothesis $H_0$, the two-sample likelihood-ratio statistic $G$ of Wilks follows a universal Chi_{r-1}^2 law, independently of the divergence chosen and of the sample sizes; the calibrated Population Stability Index (PSI) of Yurdakul and Naranjo (2021) shares the same Chi_{r-1}^2 limit and is asymptotically equivalent to the $G$-test under $H_0$. Under the drift hypothesis $H_1$, the plug-in phi-divergence is asymptotically normal with a variance computed in closed form for the one-sample, two-sample and symmetrized configurations, yielding standardized $Z$-statistics, detection boundaries, power functions and sample-size planning rules. We supply a per-category decomposition that localizes the drift on specific categories, a Benjamini--Hochberg procedure for monitoring many features simultaneously, and an explicit comparison with the heuristic PSI cut-offs of industrial practice. Two fully worked simulation examples - one one-sample with the Rényi divergence and multiple testing, one two-sample with the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and sample-size planning - illustrate every notion of the paper on realistic production data.

title: Generalization Testing of Grid Foundation Models for Power Flow and Optimal Power Flow
summary: There is growing interest in foundation models (FMs) for power grids, particularly for power flow and optimal power flow. Their usefulness depends on generalization accuracy, which existing works test on their own benchmarks. We propose a three-axis framework to test their generalization limits: changed admittance matrices of training grids, load levels, and unseen grids. We test GENCO, LUMINA and GridSFM against the DC baseline, alongside their reported limitations, and discuss theoretical reasons for their failures. Experiments reveal that adding a line degrades all FMs more than removing one, and longer lines eventually make LUMINA and fine-tuned GENCO worse than DC. All three degrade beyond their training load range, where the loading-voltage curve steepens. On unseen grids, LUMINA degrades sharply even inside its training range, and GridSFM fails on the grid farthest from it. Thus, beyond training conditions, FMs behave more like meta-models requiring test-time fine-tuning data and compute.

title: Scalable composite likelihood inference for directed probit networks
summary: We develop scalable estimation and inference for directed probit networks with correlated sending and receiving effects and residual reciprocity. An incomplete composite likelihood in two stages combines exact bivariate margins of sampled dyads and triples, avoiding integration in high dimensions and cubic enumeration. For fixed parameter dimension, criterion evaluation is linear in the number of draws. Averaging a fixed number of fits from independent index samples reduces sampling variation and allows parallel computation. We establish consistency and joint asymptotic normality with different directional rates, allowing a singular node projection when draw counts lie between the node and dyad scales. An overlap covariance accounts for network and index variation and is consistent relative to each directional variance. Independent index samples stabilize covariance estimation without refitting. The resulting procedure provides standard errors, mapped joint regions and score tests for zero variance components. Simulations show improved estimation from averaging and substantially lower computation times than default Bayesian fitting. An application to a fly brain network with 21,738 neurons demonstrates estimation and inference at a scale relevant to modern network data.

title: What Makes Good Datasets for Intelligent Multi-Modal Sensing-Communication Integration?
summary: Intelligent multi-modal sensing-communication integration, namely Synesthesia of Machines (SoM), represents an AI-native paradigm for enabling embodied intelligence and future wireless networks. Multi-modal sensing and communication foundation models developed for SoM learn cross-modal associations and generalizable environmental representations through large-scale pretraining, making the quality of pretraining datasets critical. However, existing methods lack unified evaluation of heterogeneous multi-modal data and thus struggle to meet the requirements for multi-modal pretraining dataset construction and selection. To bridge this gap, we introduce a comprehensive data evaluation framework for intelligent multi-modal sensing-communication integration. Specifically, we establish two complementary heterogeneous multi-modal data evaluation dimensions, including intrinsic data quality and validity, and model-based data utility. Furthermore, we present case studies to validate the effectiveness of the two evaluation dimensions. We also extend our analysis to investigate the impact of data quality on pretraining scaling laws and explore the value of integrating measurement and simulation data. Finally, we outline promising directions for future research on data evaluation.

title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
comment: 25 pages. An extended abstract was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival. Ancillary file: companion document with extended proofs and examples
summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+Δh(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $Δh$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|Δh\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+Δh(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

title: Site-Specific Cell Shaping: An Agentic Framework
summary: An agentic framework is proposed for cell shaping in future sixth-generation (6G) wireless network planning. Cell shaping controls the coverage and interferences of base stations (BSs) through antenna parameters configuration, providing an important means of improving coverage. In contrast to conventional approaches that reply on costly performance evaluations, the proposed framework achieves intelligent and efficient antenna configuration through a perception-reasoning-reflection loop. Specifically, a Configuration Agent combines scene information, evaluation history, and reflection feedback to generate antenna configuration proposals. Then, a ray tracing(RT)-based evaluator assesses these proposals and returns a structured performance summary. Next, a Reflection Agent interprets these results to diagnose site-specific performance deficiencies, recommend feasible configuration adjustments, and accumulate conditional experience. Through this iterative process, the framework accumulates site-specific experience and progressively refines antenna configurations without human-in-the-loop intervention. Simulations in real-world urban scenarios demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves lower outage probabilities than the considered benchmark methods, highlighting the effectiveness of agentic reasoning and reflection in translating site-specific performance feedback and accumulated experience into adaptive antenna configuration decisions.

title: Accounting for Attrition in Respondent-Driven Sampling Cohort Studies
summary: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is widely used to recruit populations lacking conventional sampling frames. Because RDS oversamples well-connected individuals, weights are commonly applied to improve representativeness. Although methods for cross-sectional RDS analyses are well developed, guidance for longitudinal studies is limited, despite additional selection bias from missed visits and dropout. We develop a framework that jointly accounts for unequal inclusion probabilities at recruitment and attrition during follow-up. The approach combines baseline RDS weights with inverse-probability-of-non-response weights estimated from observed follow-up histories, producing visit-specific weights for estimating prevalences, means, and regression parameters. We clarify when the RDS design should inform attendance models rather than being addressed only during outcome analysis. Using simulations of RDS recruitment, we assess prevalence and standardized prevalence differences under varying recruitment and attrition mechanisms, focusing on bias, variance, and confidence interval coverage. Weighting the response model by baseline RDS weights was important when an unmeasured determinant of degree also predicted response, even when it did not predict the outcome. We illustrate the framework using data from the Montreal site of Engage, a multisite RDS cohort of sexual minority men in three Canadian cities, from 2017-2023. Follow-up involved intermittent missed visits, attrition, and terminal dropout that was more common among participants with smaller networks. Our findings provide practical guidance for combining design-based and attrition adjustments to support valid inference in longitudinal RDS studies.

title: Temporal Attention-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts Guidance for Multi-Revolution Low-Thrust Rendezvous
comment: 27 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: Multi-revolution low-thrust rendezvous requires both long-duration orbital transfer and precise terminal control. This paper proposes a temporal attention-enhanced mixture-of-experts guidance law trained by deep reinforcement learning. A far-range expert acts on modified equinoctial elements, a terminal expert acts on the relative state in the target's local frame, and a learned gate blends their thrust commands. The terminal expert encodes its observation history with a Transformer to address partial observability, and the gate uses a separate encoder to account for the resulting history-dependent command. The experts are pretrained separately, the gate is trained with both experts frozen, and the complete guidance law is then fine-tuned end to end. On 600 test missions, it achieves rendezvous in every case at tolerances of 10 m and 1 m/s, reduces mean flight time and delta-v by 50.6% and 44.5% relative to distance-based hard switching, and remains successful without retraining under navigation errors, unmodeled orbital perturbations, eclipse-induced thrust outages, and thrust loss.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
summary: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

title: Integrated Co-design Framework for High-Efficiency Assembly and Integration of Small Satellites
comment: To be published in IEEE Aerospace Conference, Big Sky, MT, USA, 6-12 March, 2026
summary: The rapid growth of small-satellite constellations has increased the need for higher manufacturing throughput, lower production costs, and shorter turnaround times. This makes efficient assembly, integration, and testing (AIT) increasingly important. Building on our prior work, this paper presents an integrated design-for-AIT approach for the 65 kg Lumelite-5 satellite. The integrated approach incorporates co-designing the satellite configuration, structural interfaces, subsystem placement, harness routing, and ground support equipment to facilitate efficient AIT. Service interfaces are centralized on one satellite side to simplify electrical ground support equipment access and routing. Skeletal support interfaces are developed to retain mounted components and service interfaces when removable enclosures are opened to expose internal harness-routing paths for inspection, troubleshooting, and rework. Defined mechanical references further support controlled removal and reinstallation of sensors and components. A removable double hinge ground-support mechanism allows the top deck to open up to 180 degrees relative to the bottom deck while accommodating interconnecting-harness articulation, without introducing permanent hinge mass and complexity to the satellite. Finally, dedicated harness-routing and tie-down provisions provide predefined yet adjustable restraint locations to accommodate as built routing variations and maintain controlled harness articulation during top-deck rotation. Through this work, we demonstrate how co-designing satellite architecture and AIT processes from the early development stages can support more scalable, repeatable, and efficient constellation production.

title: Conditional Stochastic User Equilibrium as a Gibbs Distribution: Tractable Flow Laws and Exact Path-Free Sampling
summary: Treating traffic counts as data calls for the joint distribution of link flows. Stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) gives a single flow vector, and independent route choice at fixed probabilities ignores congestion feedback between travelers. Conditional stochastic user equilibrium (CSUE), in which each traveler of a finite population chooses a route by logit conditional on the routes of all others, contains this feedback but has been hard to compute with at scale. Under separable link costs and a common route-choice precision, the CSUE conditionals are those of a unique Gibbs distribution whose energy is a left-endpoint discrete congestion potential, and for continuous nondecreasing costs the law concentrates on deterministic logit SUE in the large-population limit. When the routes of each origin are the paths of an acyclic bush, retaining origin- or OD-level labels gives an unnormalized layered link-flow law with an explicit product-form multiplicity. On this representation we build a block Metropolis-Hastings sampler whose proposal is an integer version of Dial's loading under frozen costs. It leaves the CSUE law on the bush route sets invariant without enumerating paths or storing individual routes, and at stationarity the mean rejection rate of a block lies between one and two times the total variation distance between its proposal and exact conditional. In experiments, the sampler reproduces reference laws from exact enumeration and traveler-level Gibbs sampling, whereas independent route choice at frozen costs reproduces mean flows but overstates link-flow standard deviations by up to 48% and distorts correlations. On Sioux Falls, the block sampler attains 76.1 times the minimum effective sample size per CPU second of traveler-level Gibbs sampling, and on Chicago Sketch, with over one million travelers, its sampled covariance is used to assess traffic-count locations.

title: Exploration as Feedback in Model Predictive Path Integral Control
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to the 9th Annual Conference on Learning for Dynamics and Control (L4DC 2027)
summary: This paper investigates how exploration affects closed-loop stability in model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. With a warm start, MPPI optimizes a control sequence by sampling candidates around the previous solution, and their covariance, the exploration covariance, is typically tuned to balance solution quality and computational cost. Small exploration is attractive because most samples then contribute to the solution, and existing stability analyses treat reduced exploration only as a bias toward the previous solution. Whether insufficient exploration can destabilize the closed loop has therefore remained open. We show that, for linear quadratic (LQ) problems with infinitely many samples, the exploration covariance also determines the feedback gain, i.e., how strongly MPPI updates the previous solution in response to the current state. With small exploration at a fixed temperature, MPPI nearly repeats the previous solution and fails to stabilize an exponentially unstable plant. Because a single covariance governs both exploration and feedback, stability and sample efficiency are in structural conflict: stabilization requires large exploration, which leaves few samples that contribute to the solution. To resolve this conflict, we propose Stabilizing Subspace MPPI (SS-MPPI), which computes the control inputs required for stabilization and samples only the rest. For LQ problems, SS-MPPI remains stable with small exploration and is thus sample-efficient. Simulations of an inverted pendulum and a quadruped robot confirm the analysis, showing that MPPI fails under small exploration, whereas SS-MPPI remains stable even with few samples.

title: The stable false discovery rate
summary: When a discovery depends on analysis choices, a list of selected hypotheses that controls the false discovery rate (FDR) gives little indication of how easily the finding could change: the selected set may be very sensitive to a variety of analyst choices, like the target FDR level, which machine learning algorithms are used in the pipeline, the choice of test statistics, and so on. We propose that scientists should measure and control a new metric called the \emph{stable FDR} (sFDR), and give methods to control it, including simple wrappers around existing FDR analysis pipelines. sFDR is a natural continuous extension of the FDR: we assign each hypothesis an allocation between zero and one, and the sFDR equals the expected fraction of null allocation to total allocation. If one runs multiple analyses of the same data by varying different reasonable choices, allocations can be determined by simply dividing each run's selection indicators by its discovery count, then averaging across analyses and rescaling. The resulting sFDR equals the average of the ordinary FDRs of the runs, even though the runs are dependent: thus sFDR control holds under the same assumptions that the original FDR control held. (In contrast, naively reporting just fractions of times each variable was selected need not control the sFDR.) It is interpretable: hypotheses that were always selected are allocated 1 and those never selected are allocated 0. In leukemia expression and neuroimaging analyses, findings with larger allocations were more often supported in separate samples. We also develop procedures that can assign stable allocations directly from p-values, e-values, or knockoff statistics, resulting in stable-BH, stable e-BH and stable knockoff procedures. A representation by e-values describes which allocation rules control the error rate and gives ways to optimize allocations for different follow-up goals.

title: Distributed Shaping of Robot Swarms Through Spatial Moments of Arbitrary Order
summary: This paper shapes a swarm into a target pattern, such as a figure taken from an image, by controlling its spatial moments. The image is sampled into a reference configuration whose centroid and covariance set the position and principal spreads of the formation, while its higher-order moments, expressed in covariance-normalized (whitened) coordinates, encode the remaining shape. In contrast with geometric formation control, which prescribes distances, bearings, or relative positions between specific agents, this specification concerns the swarm as a whole and assigns no agent to a particular place. The key mechanism is orthogonalization in the swarm's own empirical inner product: projecting negative-gradient velocities onto the complement of low-degree polynomials sampled at the agents makes every higher-order correction preserve all lower-order moments exactly. The resulting hierarchical controller has lower triangular error dynamics and converges locally exponentially for any positive gains, so orders can be added without undoing those already achieved. A joint alternative regulates the higher moments together through a regularized Gauss--Newton step while preserving the centroid and covariance dynamics. We give bounds on the number of agents and sufficient conditions for regularity. Both controllers admit a distributed implementation that uses only relative positions and neighbor communication and retains local exponential convergence when estimation is sufficiently fast. In a distributed simulation on a sparse graph, 350 agents form an airplane from an unstructured swarm through moments up to order ten; the hierarchy reaches the full specification, while the joint law approaches it with smaller velocities.

title: On the false discovery rate of one-sided p-values under Gaussian dependence
summary: We study the false discovery rate (FDR) of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure for $K$ hypotheses at nominal level $q$ under Gaussian dependence of one-sided p-values. We ask whether the global null is least favorable after optimizing over correlation matrices. We show that the global null attains the worst-case FDR for $K\le3$ at every level. In dimension eight, an explicit mixed-null construction has FDR $21q/20$ for $0<q<1/2$. It exceeds the global-null maximum for all sufficiently small $q$, by a uniform extension of the known fixed-matrix small-level Simes bound. For $0<q<1/2$, we identify eight as the first inflation dimension in the monotone rank-one class and prove that $21q/20$ is its exact eight-dimensional maximum. In the same level range, the sharp multiplicative bound over all dimensions in this class is twice the omega constant $w = W(1)$, where $W$ is the Lambert $W$ function. This bound is approached as the dimension increases. We also give scale conditions for stability around the independence benchmark $m_0q/K$, where $m_0$ is the number of true nulls, and obtain a dimension-free upper bound of $q+q^2/2+O(q^3)$ at small levels under the global null with nonpositive correlations.

title: Hardware-Friendly Plug-and-Play MVDR Beamforming for Microphone Arrays: Algorithm, Prototype, and System-Level Feasibility
summary: Beamforming has been widely recognized for its spatial filtering capability in speech signal processing, enabling effective interference rejection and signal enhancement. The performance of adaptive beamforming methods, e.g., the conventional minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) beamforming, often deteriorate significantly in complex and dynamic acoustic environments. Part of the reason is that such conventional beamforming ignores the intrinsic characteristics of speech. To address this issue, this paper proposes Plug-and-Play Minimum Variance Distortionless Response (PnP-MVDR) algorithm, which integrates data-driven speech prior information into the MVDR framework to enhance robustness against non-stationary noise while maintaining its interpretability. The PnP-MVDR framework supports joint interaction of signal processing and deep learning methods and is designed to be compatible with modern DSP-NPU architectures, making it hardware-friendly for potential edge deployment. Beyond the algorithmic innovation, we have developed a complete microphone beamforming system to validate practical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms traditional and deep learning-based baselines, establishing PnP-MVDR as an effective and deployable solution for edge audio scenarios.

title: Probability of Success under Population Shift for Phase III Trial Planning
summary: Probability of success (PoS) is widely used to inform go/no-go decisions for phase III trials based on phase II evidence. Conventional PoS calculations, however, implicitly assume that baseline covariate distributions are identical across phases. When covariate shift exists between phase II and phase III populations, unadjusted PoS may be biased and lead to miscalibrated decision-making. We propose a Bayesian framework for PoS evaluation that explicitly accounts for covariate shift between phase II and III population prior to phase III initiation. The method adopts a transportability perspective, adjusting phase II evidence to reflect an anticipated phase III target population using available target covariate information. The framework accommodates both individual-level and aggregate-level phase III covariate data. Simulation studies demonstrate that, compared with the conventional approach, the proposed method improves PoS accuracy and decision calibration when covariate shift is present, while maintaining comparable performance when populations are aligned. We illustrate the proposed methodology using clinical trial data from systemic lupus erythematosus.

title: Sensing with OFDM Signals: How Do the Constellations Affect the Sensing Accuracy?
summary: This paper investigates how communication constellations affect joint range-velocity estimation with data-bearing orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signals. To this end, starting from the continuous-time sensing process, we derive a discrete observation model and specify its validity conditions. For multiple targets with unknown delays, Doppler shifts, and complex gains, the complete Fisher information matrix (FIM) admits a structural factorization separating deterministic channel derivatives from random symbol-energy weights. This structure yields a Jensen-type lower bound on the average conditional Cramer-Rao bound (CRB), which is attained exactly by constant-modulus constellations. Single-target closed-form expressions further reveal the dependence of the bounds on the transmitted energy distribution and physical OFDM parameters. We also formulate two-dimensional fast Fourier transform (FFT), concentrated maximum-likelihood (ML), and sliding-subarray multiple signal classification (MUSIC) processing under the derived observation model. Numerical results support the theoretical optimality of constant-modulus constellations but also show that the CRB gap between phase-shift keying (PSK) and quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) becomes negligible when the numbers of subcarriers and OFDM symbols are considerably large. The performance of ML estimation closely approaches the derived bounds, which confirms the effectiveness of the theoretical analysis. FFT processing exhibits grid-induced error floors. In the considered scenarios, MUSIC provides lower estimation errors than FFT and exhibits a more pronounced constellation dependence.

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
summary: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $dσ^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $σ^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

title: Active-Element Configuration for Energy-Efficient Secure Near-Field ISAC With Hybrid RISs
summary: Hybrid active-passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (HRISs) are promising for secure near-field integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) through selective signal amplification and spherical-wave beam focusing. However, fixed active-element layouts limit flexibility in exploiting element-dependent near-field channels while balancing secrecy performance, sensing accuracy, and circuit power consumption. This paper develops a joint active-element configuration and transmission design for a large-aperture HRIS-assisted system, where sensing targets act as potential eavesdroppers. The design adapts both the number and spatial distribution of active elements by exploiting near-field phase and attenuation variations. We establish a bidirectional signal and power model with full-aperture reflection and active-subset amplification for downlink signals and uplink echoes. Based on the derived three-dimensional localization Cramér-Rao bound, we formulate a mixed-integer non-convex secrecy energy efficiency (SEE) maximization problem under user-rate, localization, and power constraints. To solve this problem, we propose an alternating optimization framework combining successive convex approximation, a penalty convex-concave procedure, and full-aperture reweighted group-sparse selection. The selection method scores and ranks elements to generate binary candidate configurations without exhaustive search. After refining continuous HRIS variables for each candidate, we select the feasible configuration with the highest genuine SEE. Simulation results demonstrate higher SEE with lower base station transmit power than fixed-layout HRIS schemes and a fully passive RIS baseline.

title: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence
summary: We initiate the study of estimating a discrete distribution with respect to the hockey-stick divergence from independent samples. We provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the minimax expected loss in terms of the alphabet size, the number of samples, and the divergence parameter. The upper bounds are achieved by add-constant estimators, while the lower bound is derived via a Bayes risk argument. Both upper bounds and lower bounds reveal a transition between polynomial and exponential regimes as the parameters of the problem vary.

title: XLSAR-Bench: Towards Extremely Large SAR Imagery Understanding of MLLMs
summary: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153$\times$7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.

title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
summary: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

title: Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer
summary: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth. We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

title: Statistical and Optimization Models for Generating Electricity in Energy Markets
summary: Electricity generation has become a remunerative avenue for new investments, particularly in the area of renewable energy resources. This paper introduces a framework for integrating statistical methods with optimization modeling to improve decision support in electricity generation. The analysis begins by evaluating the success of mini-grid projects installed across the globe using both a probit and a Bayesian hierarchical model to estimate the probability of project success. Furthermore, we provide a multi-resource optimization framework for determining the optimal profit in electricity generation while reducing carbon emissions in production facilities. We also analyze the impact of a battery energy storage system and bidding behavior in the Alberta electricity market by constructing a mixed-integer self-scheduling model that determines optimal charging and discharging strategies. Numerical experiments show how storage systems can enhance energy arbitrage profitability and influence market clearing prices. Finally, we propose a Stochastic Dynamic Programming (SDP) model to maximize profit in electricity generation while accounting for price volatility. Integrating statistical methods with optimization-based modeling reveals great value in achieving more effective, profitable, and clean energy systems.

title: Pixel-KWS: Rendered-Glyph Representations for Orthographically Robust Open-Vocabulary Keyword Spotting
summary: Open-vocabulary keyword spotting (KWS) allows users to enroll arbitrary keywords at inference time. However, character and phoneme-based text encoders rely on fixed symbol vocabularies learned during training, limiting their ability to handle unseen or visually similar symbols such as homoglyphs, l33tspeak substitutions, and accented characters. We propose PIXEL-KWS, an open-vocabulary KWS framework that represents characters through rendered glyphs rather than learned embedding lookups. We render each character as a grayscale image and encode it with a lightweight CNN, enabling the text encoder to generalize from visual form rather than a fixed vocabulary. On LibriPhrase, PIXEL-KWS and its matched character-based counterpart achieve 9.57% and 9.55% EER on LibriPhrase-hard, 0.43% and 0.41% EER on LibriPhrase-easy, outperforming all published baselines without pre-training or synthetic data. PIXEL-KWS provides substantially greater robustness to both homoglyph and l33tspeak symbol-level perturbations. These results highlight glyph-based representations as a simple and effective approach for robust open-vocabulary KWS in practical settings.

title: Limited Follow Up Overlap in Causal Survival Analysis: Censoring-Adjusted Weighting for Restricted Mean Survival Time
summary: Overlap weighting addresses limited treatment overlap by targeting individuals for whom treatment assignment is uncertain. With right censored outcomes, however, adequate treatment overlap does not ensure adequate follow up. We show that the overlap weighted restricted mean survival time difference can have an infinite semiparametric efficiency bound even under randomized treatment and pointwise censoring positivity. We propose censoring adjusted overlap (CO) weighting, that accounts jointly for treatment assignment and the probability of remaining under observation through the restriction horizon. CO approaches ordinary overlap weighting as the strength of the follow up adjustment decreases and progressively downweights covariate profiles with weak follow up. We derive the efficient influence function and show that it is uniformly bounded without requiring censoring survival probabilities to be uniformly bounded away from zero. A cross fitted one step estimator is asymptotically normal with consistently estimated variance under follow up weighted nuisance rate conditions. Simulations show little difference from overlap weighting when follow up is adequate, but substantially greater stability as follow up deteriorates. An analysis of the Rotterdam breast cancer cohort illustrates both the protection against weak follow up and the potential cost in precision.

title: Optimal Coordination of Multiple Ancillary Service Provisions in Active Distribution Networks
summary: We propose a multi-rate model predictive control (MPC) framework for coordinating primary frequency control (PFC), automatic generation control (AGC), and voltage control (VC) in active distribution networks. The framework allocates distributed energy resource (DER) flexibility among these three ancillary services while retaining their different update rates. To account for the intertemporal flexibility of electric vehicle aggregations and aggregations of buildings with thermostatically controlled loads (TCLs), we incorporate time-varying power-energy envelopes into our multi-rate MPC formulation. These constraints couple the combined PFC and AGC response to the demand-side flexibility available later in the prediction horizon. Furthermore, the input-multirate structure enables coordinated ancillary service provision by DERs with different response dynamics. The controller optimizes the three services together, allowing fast regulation to be coordinated with the developing slow response within the available DER flexibility. We demonstrate the coordinated provision of the three ancillary services through closed-loop simulations on a modified IEEE 33-bus system using a nonlinear differential-algebraic model.

title: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
summary: Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle. The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

title: Fault Diagnosis and Fault-Tolerant Operation Strategy for Triple-Port Hydrogen Production System
summary: The multi-port converter offers significant advantages in sustainable energy-based hydrogen production, such as high energy density and wide application potential. As the core energy hub in these systems, the multi-port hydrogen converter demands high reliability. However, its numerous switches and complex operation increase the risk of failure. Currently, there are no effective fault diagnosis or fault tolerance solutions for these systems. Current fault diagnosis methods for two-port and multi-port converters rely on many sensors, have low accuracy, and cannot handle multi-switch faults. Additionally, existing fault tolerance strategies fall short in maintaining stable power for the electrolyzer and do not allow capacity sharing among ports. This paper proposes a fault diagnosis method for open-circuit faults in a triple-port hydrogen converter and a corresponding fault-tolerant operating strategy. By optimizing a random forest algorithm with a sparrow search algorithm, high-precision multi-switch fault diagnosis is achieved using only three current sensors. Fault-tolerant operation of the system is achieved through an auxiliary switch after a failure. Additionally, power sharing between output ports can be realized. This ensures the efficient and stable operation of the hydrogen production system. The effectiveness of this solution has been validated through simulations and experiments.

title: Tight Sequential Confidence Intervals for Online Kernel Regression
summary: We characterize, in the worst case over kernels, the sharp minimax width of online confidence intervals for elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This resolves the open problem posed by Vakili et al. (2021) in its original discrete-time form. A learner observes $y_i=f(x_i)+ε_i$ at adaptively chosen points, with $\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B$ and i.i.d. $R$-sub-Gaussian noise, and reports the interval $|f(x)-μ_n(x)|\leρ_n(δ)σ_n(x)$, where $μ_n$ and $σ_n$ are the posterior mean and standard deviation of a surrogate Gaussian process model with regularization parameter $λ$. Writing $ρ_n^*(δ)$ for the minimax confidence width for a fixed kernel, we show that, for the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel, all sufficiently large $n$, and all $δ\in(0,1/4]$, $ρ_n^*(δ)\asymp B+(R/λ)\sqrt{γ_n+\log(1/δ)}$, where $γ_n$ is the maximal information gain and grows polynomially in $n$. Building on Lattimore (2023), we construct an adaptive design on a fixed two-dimensional domain for which, under Gaussian noise, the normalized error at a prespecified point is $Ω(B+(R/λ)\sqrt{γ_n})$ with constant probability. This rules out the conjectured polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and online designs.

title: Hydrogen in Practice: A Global Review of Demonstration Projects from Production to Integration
summary: Hydrogen technology has the potential to address various challenges related to integrating low- and zero-carbon energy sources, as well as achieving carbon neutrality. It provides valuable solutions for transitioning to net-zero emission energy systems on a global scale. The implementation of hydrogen production and integration demonstration projects has received significant attention around the world and strong support from governments, highlighting the crucial role of such initiatives in the advancement of hydrogen energy. However, research in this area remains limited, particularly in terms of comprehensive and systematic reviews of industrial practices under real-world conditions. To bridge this gap, this article provides an in-depth review of hydrogen production, storage, and industrial applications, summarizing key features of thirteen exemplary hydrogen demonstration projects from around the world. The goal is to offer insights and guidance for the large-scale deployment of hydrogen energy while identifying potential technological pathways for the future.

title: Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer
summary: In this paper, we propose a conditional asset pricing transformer (CAP-T) that captures nonlinear interactions among firms through attention to forecast excess returns. In the first stage, a transformer estimates conditional expected returns, and kernel-weighted principal component analysis of its residuals estimates the local factor loading space. Projecting the conditional mean onto this space separates factor risk compensation from conditional mispricing. Then, in the second stage, separate transformers learn these two components, whose predictions are combined to forecast returns. As a result, the proposed framework decomposes returns into conditional mispricing, factor risk compensation, a centered factor component, and an unpredictable innovation. We establish approximation and generalization bounds and characterize how first-stage prediction errors propagate through local factor estimation and component learning, providing statistical guaranties for conditional mispricing, factor loadings, and factor risk premia. Finally, simulations and empirical studies demonstrate the predictive and interpretive benefits of the proposed method.

title: DyTransRM: A Unified Simulation-to-Real Framework for Dynamic Radio Map Prediction
summary: Dynamic radio map (RM) prediction enables proactive wireless network control by forecasting future propagation conditions from historical observations. However, collecting temporally continuous and spatially dense real-world RMs is prohibitively expensive, while models trained on large-scale simulated data often suffer from limited transferability to real environments. To address this issue, we propose DyTransRM, a unified simulation-to-real framework for dynamic RM prediction under sparse real-world measurements. DyTransRM first introduces RadioCLIP to learn physics-semantic representations by aligning environmental evolution with the corresponding propagation evolution, thereby improving both prediction accuracy and cross-domain transferability. To further bridge the simulation-to-real gap, SparseUOT employs sparse-mask simulation refinement to mimic realistic measurement patterns and unbalanced optimal transport to selectively align compatible propagation representations across domains. Experiments on RadioMapMotion and real-world datasets demonstrate that RadioCLIP achieves an NMSE of 0.0018 and an RMSE of 0.012 in simulation-domain prediction. After sparse real-domain adaptation, DyTransRM achieves an NMSE of 0.023, RMSE of 0.079, and MAE of 0.064, outperforming representative adaptation baselines without requiring spatially complete real RMs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DyTransRM for transferring simulation-learned dynamic propagation knowledge to practical sparse-measurement scenarios.

title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
summary: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

title: Representing Differential Inclusions as Monads: A Framework for Compositional Controller Synthesis
summary:
Sequential composition of safety-certified controllers for hybrid and non-smooth robotic systems is well studied piecewise. Yet no existing framework reduces this question to a single algebraic condition. We construct a \emph{trajectory monad} for Filippov-regular differential inclusions. Its Kleisli category treats controllers as morphisms and sequential execution as trajectory concatenation. Control Barrier Function (CBF) certification, a guarantee of forward invariance, corresponds to a sub-monad of this category. Joint safety of composed controllers then follows from one algebraic condition. All controllers must land in a common sub-monad, which is closed under the monad multiplication.
  The sub-monad condition recasts recasts existing CBF composition practice categorically. It explains why a smooth intersection of multiple barriers supports safe composition, while enforcing barriers phase by phase does not. For the phase-by-phase case, we derive a closed-form Bernoulli model of the failure rate. We validate it over a randomized sweep of 3{,}000 instances. The same sweep shows that the standard baseline degrades under constraint conflict as the barrier count grows. This baseline enforces all barriers simultaneously as constraints in a single quadratic program (QP). We instantiate the framework on a four-mode piecewise-affine system and on a unicycle reduced-order model over heterogeneous terrain.

title: Certified Algorithms for Gaussian Location Mixture NPMLEs via Discretized Gradient Flows
summary: We study the computation of approximate nonparametric maximum likelihood estimators (NPMLEs) for Gaussian location mixtures in arbitrary dimension $d\ge 1$ via the Fisher-Rao gradient flow. We provide a certified algorithm based on an entropic proximal discretization of the flow which, given a sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, returns an absolutely continuous mixing measure $\tildeμ$ admitting an exact finite-dimensional representation and satisfying $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\tildeμ})\le\varepsilon$. For almost every dataset $X_1,\cdots, X_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying $n>2(d+1)(m+1)^2$, where $m$ is the number of support points of the NPMLE, the algorithm requires $O(n\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d+2}(1/\varepsilon))$ time. En route, we also establish results on the well-posedness and convergence properties of the continuous-time Fisher--Rao flow. In particular, initializing the flow at the uniform probability measure on a ball containing the convex hull of the observations, we show that $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{μ_t})=O(\log t/t)$. We also establish that, for almost every dataset satisfying the same condition on $n$ as above, the set of global maxima of the optimal score is the same as the support of the NPMLE, and the Hessian of the optimal score is nondegenerate at these points, extending a result of (Polyanskiy-Sellke, 2025) to higher dimensions.

title: UACS: Uncertainty-Aware Clustering and Sparse Parameter Estimation for Multi-Condition Wheel Center Force
summary: Accurate wheel center force (WCF) estimation is important for vehicle durability analysis and condition monitoring, whereas direct measurement requires dedicated transducers and increases instrumentation cost and complexity. As a result, soft sensors have attracted considerable attention as a practical alternative. However, developing reliable soft sensors remains challenging due to varying working conditions, unknown condition relationships, and high-dimensional model representations. This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware clustering and sparse parameter estimation framework (UACS) for WCF signal estimation under diverse and unlabeled working conditions. A MISO-FIR model is first constructed using easily accessible sensor signals to estimate the unmeasurable force signal. The uncertainty of estimated parameters is quantified through confidence ellipsoids, and pairwise hypothesis testing is developed to identify statistically similar working conditions. Based on these uncertainty-aware comparisons, working conditions are grouped in an unsupervised manner, and sparse parameter estimation is performed within each cluster. The UACS framework simultaneously reduces the number of required models and active parameters while maintaining estimation accuracy. Experiments using real-world vehicle data demonstrate that the UACS framework achieves estimation accuracy comparable to condition-specific models while substantially reducing the number of required models and outperforming conventional distance-based clustering approaches.

title: Count Constraints and Conditional Benchmarks for Roster-Based Network Reconstruction
comment: 25 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Builds on the matched-input comparison in arXiv:2501.10675v3; adds complete-constraint accounting, conditional benchmarks with a characterization, independent density and blockmodel studies, and a saved-fit conditional comparison
summary: When everyone reports contact counts for known groups, roster-based aggregated relational data (ARD) can determine individual links. In our sparse circular design with 40 nodes and eight groups, the complete counts fix 35.6% of realized edges on average. Zero counts alone exclude 91.1% of nonedges on average, and the full set of counts raises that share to 91.7%. We assess ranking on the unresolved pairs by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Uniform weighting of compatible graphs yields higher mean AUC than the direct scores from either a circular latent-position fit or a nuclear-norm fit. In a follow-up analysis, using the same fitted probabilities to weight compatible graphs reverses the comparison for the circular fit. With the generating circular form and interaction strength supplied, its mean AUC exceeds uniform by 0.016-0.019 across three paired density settings. The gain is 0.007 under a stochastic blockmodel, where the circular form is misspecified. Nuclear-norm plug-in scores remain below uniform in mean AUC. For independent Bernoulli edges with fixed probabilities strictly between zero and one, we characterize when an oracle using the true probabilities gives the same edge marginals as uniform weighting for every feasible count array. This occurs exactly when the conditional graph law is uniform on every such array, or equivalently when log odds are additive in node-by-group effects. We recommend reporting fixed edge states, ranking on unresolved pairs, and generating-probability error separately.

title: Leveraging Dual-Process Theory for Multimodal Multiparty Turn-Taking Prediction
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Preprint submitted to IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing
summary: In multiparty conversations, a pause does not always mean a speaker has finished, and another voice does not necessarily indicate a change in who holds the conversational floor. Reliable turn-taking therefore requires recognising not only whether a speaker is ready to yield the floor, but also when a possible transition deserves attention. We propose a dual-process-inspired framework that separates continuous candidate discovery from selective verification. A fast, recall-oriented stage identifies plausible transition points. In contrast, a deliberative stage combines acoustic, linguistic, speaker-related, and predicted future-activity evidence, together with multimodal cues where available, to reject false candidates and refine transition timing. We evaluate the framework through three distinct tasks: SHIFT/HOLD classification at supplied decision points, verification of automatically generated candidates, and continuous discovery and localisation of floor transfers. On VoxConverse, we derive action-aware turn-taking events from speaker-diarization annotations to examine unconstrained conversations with varying numbers of speakers. Multi-TPC provides complementary evaluation of controlled triadic interactions using speech, gaze, motion, and prosodic information. The findings reveal that identifying plausible transitions is considerably easier than reliably confirming and localising genuine floor transfers, while the contribution of individual evidence sources varies across conversational settings. These results highlight the importance of treating multiparty turn-taking as a continuous discovery-and-verification problem rather than classification at predefined boundaries.

title: Subarchetypal Analysis: A Semi-Supervised Framework for Archetypal Analysis
summary: In this work, we introduce subarchetypal analysis, a new semi-supervised framework for Archetype Analysis (AA) and Archetypoid Analysis (ADA) based on subsets of observations from which archetypal profiles are generated. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first subset-constrained framework for archetypal analysis. Classical AA and ADA are recovered as special cases, and the location result for archetypes is extended to the proposed framework. The generating subsets may be defined a priori by the user to incorporate external knowledge, or determined from intrinsic properties of the data or the underlying problem structure. As an illustration of the latter, we consider efficient subarchetypes within Data Envelopment Analysis, where the subsets are determined by the geometry of the efficient frontier. We develop and implement algorithms for subarchetypal analysis in both multivariate and functional settings, available in an R package. The proposed methods are compared with constrained clustering, group-wise archetypal analysis, and classical unconstrained AA and ADA, and their practical usefulness is demonstrated through applications to business, sports analytics, and human development data.

title: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
summary: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

title: RADISH: A Robust Covariate-Adaptive Trial Design with Historical Control Borrowing
summary: Incorporating historical controls into randomized clinical trials can improve statistical efficiency and alleviate enrollment challenges by reducing the need for concurrent controls, particularly when their recruitment is ethically or logistically challenging. These gains depend on comparability between the historical and concurrent controls. Many dynamic borrowing methods assess compatibility for the overall study populations and apply the same borrowing decision to every participant, even when comparability varies with participant covariates. We propose RADISH, Robust Adaptive Discrepancy-Informed Shrinkage for Historical Borrowing, a covariate-adaptive design that assesses compatibility at the individual participant level and incorporates robust borrowing into sequential randomization and final inference. Under the stated regularity conditions, the RADISH estimator is asymptotically normal and supports asymptotically valid Wald inference. Simulation studies, including semi-synthetic simulation studies based on the two real-world randomized trials, show that RADISH improves efficiency and assigns fewer participants to the control group when the historical and concurrent controls are compatible. As incompatibility increases, RADISH progressively reduces borrowing and approaches a concurrent-only design and analysis.

title: AC Assessment of DC Power Flow Screening for Data Center Hosting Capacity and Siting
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting
summary: A screening procedure based on direct current (DC) power flow estimates the data center hosting capacity of a candidate bus, termed the DC-screened capacity, and selects the generator commitment that supports it. This paper assesses that estimate under the alternating current (AC) network model. With the selected commitment fixed, an AC optimal power flow reoptimizes dispatch and voltages to find the largest data center load the bus can carry, termed the AC-assessed capacity. On a synthetic Texas system with 123 buses, the DC-screened capacity exceeds the AC-assessed capacity at 113 buses. Across all 123, the ratio of DC-screened to AC-assessed capacity has a median of 143% (a 43% overestimate) and a maximum of 1,070%. At these 113 buses, the DC-screened capacity violates a branch apparent power limit or a generator reactive power limit in the AC model, two limits the DC model omits. The overestimate changes decisions: a 1-GW project passes DC screening at every bus but exceeds the AC-assessed capacity at 37, and the bus ranked first by DC screening has 205.5 MW less AC-assessed capacity than the bus ranked second. Reporting the AC-assessed capacity beside each DC-screened capacity lets planners reject oversized projects or choose better sites.

title: orderStatMoments: Exact Means, Variances, and Covariances of Order Statistics in R
comment: 46 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. The R package is available at https://github.com/ZWuLab/orderStatMoments
summary:
Calculating the moments, i.e., means, variances, and covariances, of the order statistics of a sample is critical, as they are foundations for order-statistics-based estimation and inference problems. In the early literature, the exact covariance matrices were tabulated only up to the sample size of 50 under normality. Recent software either provides exact calculation only for the means and variances of single order statistics, or obtains the covariances by approximations.
  We create the R package orderStatMoments to calculate the exact values of these moments for any ranks and any sample size. It covers thirteen built-in distribution families, specified by name and parameters as in R, and allows for continuous distributions defined by the user under relatively weak conditions. It also calculates the moments of any linear combination of order statistics, including sample quantiles, and Lloyd's best linear unbiased estimators with their variances.
  The work makes two contributions. First, the package provides the exact covariances between order statistics, which no software we found does. Second, we design methods based on the statistical properties of order statistics critical for ultra accurate computing at large sample sizes and various distributions. The accuracy is verified against closed forms at sample sizes up to $n = 10^6$, against the permutation identities on full matrices, and against 556 cells tabulated in seven publications, where it identified some errors far beyond the stated accuracy. A comparison with five R packages and Python's SciPy shows advantages of this package. Computing is efficient, with a time nearly independent of the sample size.

title: Impact of Wind-Solar-Battery Growth on Electricity Prices: Reserve Scarcity and Transmission Congestion
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE GECA 2027
summary: This paper asks whether sequential wind, solar, and battery storage additions that eliminate unserved energy also remove modeled reserve scarcity and transmission congestion. Thirty-one cumulative portfolio states are evaluated on a modified IEEE 24-bus system for a constructed stressed day using a 24-hour day-ahead unit commitment model with network constraints, co-optimized energy and upward reserve, chronological battery storage, and an approximation of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas operating reserve demand curve. The thermal baseline has 106 MWh of unserved energy, whereas 450 MW of wind is sufficient to serve all demand. However, with 1,500 MW of wind, the hourly modeled reserve scarcity price still reaches \$5,000/MWh because wind output declines after the system peak. Adding 1,800 MW of solar reduces the load weighted daily average modeled reserve scarcity price from \$1,136.2/MWh to \$101.2/MWh and confines modeled reserve scarcity to three evening hours.
