Adding 250 MW/1,000 MWh of battery storage further lowers the average to \$4.3/MWh and reduces wind curtailment from 631 MWh to 306 MWh. Transmission congestion nevertheless remains: all residual wind curtailment occurs at bus 21, wind capture prices at buses 21 and 23 differ by \$31.8/MWh, and identical battery storage plants yield normalized net energy market revenues of \$201/(MW$\cdot$day) and \$121/(MW$\cdot$day) at buses 19 and 21, respectively. These results show that unserved energy, modeled reserve scarcity, and locational congestion effects measure distinct operating conditions and should be evaluated separately but interpreted together.

title: Testing Cross-Sectional Dependence in Clustered Data
summary: In clustered data, cross-sectional dependence within clusters can be characterized as weak, semi-strong, or strong. This paper proposes a simple test to identify the specific nature of this dependence in linear regression models. By exploiting the variation in cluster sizes, our approach detects the underlying dependence structure in a computationally simple and robust manner. We develop a test statistic that is shown to be asymptotically chi-square distributed under the null hypothesis of weak dependence. Simulation studies and an empirical illustration using India's Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) data for 2022-23 demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed test.

title: Low-Voltage Ride-Through in AI Data Centers via Coordinated Battery and Computing Load Control
summary: The ability of large AI data centers to ride through grid voltage sags is critical to power system stability and reliability. This paper frames data center low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) as a DC-link power balance problem. Once the rectifier reaches its current limit, the power drawn from the grid decreases in proportion to the grid voltage. The DC-link capacitor can supply the resulting power deficit only briefly before the DC-link voltage falls low enough to trigger undervoltage protection tripping. To address this issue, this paper proposes effective control strategies for coordinating uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery and computing load curtailment to offset the power deficit and enable LVRT at minimum control cost. Three control scenarios are studied: UPS battery support alone, computing load curtailment alone, and the coordinated use of both resources. Electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations using the TAMU-ERCOT AI data center model demonstrate that battery support and the coordinated strategy achieve LVRT for all tested sags, including a near-zero-voltage fault, while load curtailment alone rides through moderate voltage sags.

title: Two approaches of estimation for a tempered fractional Brownian motion with drift
summary: We investigate the problem of estimation for a tempered fractional Brownian motion with drift of the form: $X_t=μt + σB_{H,λ}(t)$, for all $t\geq 0$. Based on discrete observations of $X$ and by using the method of moments with the ergodic theorem, we construct estimators of the drift parameter $μ\in\R$ and noise parameters $ σ^2,H,λ\in(0,\infty)$. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators, including convergence in probability, almost sure convergence, and asymptotic normality. Finally, by using Gladyshev's results \cite{gladyshev1961new} we provide some consistent alternative estimators of $σ^2$, $H$ and $λ$, when $μ=0$ and $H\in (0,1)$.

title: Behavioral Denoising: A New Perspective on Nonlinear Behavioral Control Inspired by Closed-Form Diffusion Policies
summary: Diffusion policies have become a dominant approach to imitation learning in robotics. Recent work suggests that, in the low-data regime, they largely retrieve or combine the demonstrated actions, which the closed-form diffusion policy does explicitly. This closely resembles behavioral control, where future inputs are formed as linear combinations of recorded trajectories. In this work, we make this connection precise: we show that the weights with which the closed-form diffusion policy combines the demonstrated actions are the unique solution of a regularized behavioral control problem. Building on this connection, we propose an algorithm, termed $χ^2$-projected behavioral denoising, which is a training-free method that combines nearby trajectory data with a limit on extrapolation when the data offer little support. It shows encouraging results on four nonlinear control tasks compared to recent nonlinear behavioral control methods. We hope that this connection offers a useful perspective for understanding both data-driven control and diffusion policies. Code and more visualizations can be found at https://github.com/RoboticExplorationLab/behavioral-denoising.

title: Dependence measures as spectral risk measures
summary: For a bivariate copula $C$ with $(U,V)\sim C$, the conditional distribution functions $L_t=\partial_1C(U,t)$ are random variables with means $t$, so that measures of directed dependence become risk functionals. The absolute Lorenz curves of the variables $L_t$ form the rearranged copula $C^\uparrow$. In this picture Chatterjee's rank correlation $ξ$ is a squared Sobolev seminorm and the rearranged Spearman correlation an $L^1$ norm of $C^\uparrow-Π$, and both arise from one spectral risk measure, applied either to the conditional laws of $V$ or to the laws of $L_t$. The resulting classes $ω_φ$ and $κ_φ$ of spectral dependence measures have mirror-image axiomatic properties. For every spectrum we determine the exact upper bound of $κ_φ$ in terms of $ξ$, and we prove sharp inequalities between $ξ$, $κ_φ$ and the values of $C^\uparrow$, which show how little global measures say about the tails. For plug-in estimators based on the empirical checkerboard copula we obtain consistency, rates and a resolution limit, and a simulation study shows that tail-localised measures separate copulas with identical $ξ$. An application to large credit portfolios illustrates the results.

title: Topology-Transferable Detection of Deep-Learning False Data Injection Attacks Through Residual-Energy Separation
summary: Deep learning (DL) false data injection (FDI) attacks can evade both bad data detection (BDD) and data-driven (DD) detectors in AC power system state estimation (SE), and DD detectors lose effectiveness after a topology change unless they are retrained. We argue that BDD fails in its decision rule, not in its statistic. A reconstruction-based DL generator pursues stealth by fitting the measurements closely, and because such a generator tends to act as a denoiser, the attacked residual energy can fall into the lower tail that BDD never inspects. The weighted-least-squares (WLS) residual applies the same projector construction to the noise and to the attack error, and under a spectral suppression condition we prove that the expected residual energies of normal and attacked measurements are separated by a topology-independent margin. Empirically, a rule learned on the residual energy at one topology transfers without retraining and keeps mean cross-topology F1 above 0.98 on the IEEE 14-bus, 39-bus, 57-bus, and 118-bus systems, while a raw measurement DD detector collapses.

title: Weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift: process limits, estimated weights and efficiency
summary: Weighted split conformal prediction handles covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio $v=dQ_X/dP_X$; its training-conditional coverage is a functional of the self-normalized weighted empirical distribution function $\hat F_m$, and we study the process $\sqrt m(\hat F_m-F_Q)$. It converges in $\ell^\infty$ to the Gaussian process $W(G(t))-F_Q(t)W(K^2)$, with $G(t)=\mathbb{E}_Q[v\mathbf{1}\{S\le t\}]$ and $K^2=1+χ^2(Q\|P)$, if and only if $χ^2(Q\|P)<\infty$ (for non-degenerate scores); $\sup v$ plays no role. The limit gives the joint law of the coverage across levels, consistent bootstraps, inflations asymptotically exact uniformly in the level, and Berry-Esseen-type rates. With estimated ratios, a uniform expansion remains valid when the estimate uses the calibration covariates; the estimation error enters through a covariance term that can reduce the variance below the oracle's, and a pairs bootstrap reproduces it. When the ratio is known, the weighted conformal threshold is semiparametrically efficient if and only if the ratio and the coverage indicator are uncorrelated under the test distribution, with an explicit efficient correction otherwise. When $χ^2(Q\|P)=\infty$, the ratio has a regularly varying tail of index $p\in(1,2)$ and the score decouples from it in the far tail, the finite-dimensional limits are $p$-stable at the rate $m^{1-1/p}$ up to a slowly varying factor.

title: Rethinking Post-Training for Expressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
summary: Zero-shot voice cloning typically emphasizes preserving the timbre and prosodic characteristics of a reference speaker. However, in real-world use, speech should adapt its delivery to the target text rather than remain tied to a fixed speaking style. In this work, we formulate this problem as text-adaptive prosody synthesis for zero-shot voice cloning and study how post-training can endow a cloning model with this capability. We develop a three-stage framework. First, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a cold start by aligning the model with text-appropriate expressive speech. Second, Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) jointly optimizes prosodic expressiveness, acoustic quality, intelligibility, and speaker similarity. Finally, context-conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) enables self-improvement by transferring expressive behavior from strong-reference to weak-reference conditions. On Qwen3-TTS, our framework improves Emotion from 18.5 to 81.2 and Paralinguistics from 38.4 to 73.9. Extensive ablations validate the role of each stage.

title: Honest confidence sets under experiment-level failure
summary: An experiment-level failure replaces the joint observation law while preserving the target. We study honest confidence sets when a declared upper bound on failure probability equals the allowed noncoverage probability. For a Uniform support endpoint and a Gaussian mean on fixed compact parameter intervals, every honest deterministic procedure has full-range worst-case expected diameter under arbitrary or absolutely continuous joint failures. Independent randomisation gives sharp minimax risks of $(2+o(1))\log N/N$ for the endpoint in $[1,2]$ and $(2σ+o(1))(\log N/N)^{1/2}$ for the mean with known variance $σ^2$. A failure distribution shared by many targets forces average clean-state noncoverage to decrease with expected diameter. One-sided local Kullback--Leibler bounds then yield lower bounds with logarithmic factors. The endpoint experiment also has a sharp deterministic frontier as the remaining error budget vanishes. Under exchangeable failures without ties, observation order recovers both randomised benchmark rates deterministically. In a reference-calibrated roster, we derive the randomised minimax reliability rate. A prespecified reference reserve of logarithmic size permits deterministic attainment of the same order on a subclass whose conditionally independent reserved responses have probabilities bounded away from zero and one in every state.

title: Hermitian Positive Definite Neural Networks for Matrix-CFAR Geometric Signal Detection in Nonhomogeneous Clutter
summary: Matrix information geometry (MIG) detectors exploit the Riemannian geometry of Hermitian positive definite (HPD) matrices to achieve robust object detection in nonhomogeneous clutter. The matrix constant false alarm rate (matrix-CFAR) method is a representative MIG detector that relies on the geometric structures with respect to specific metrics. In most cases, computing representative HPD covariance matrices requires numerical methods, typically involving computationally intensive iterative optimization algorithms. Although explicit formulas are available for certain cases, such as the log-Euclidean (LE) mean, they are generally unavailable for many other matrix means and medians. To address this challenge, we propose integrating the Hermitian positive definite neural network (HPDNet) into the matrix-CFAR framework, replacing conventional numerical optimization procedures with a learned, geometry-preserving mapping that directly estimates representative HPD covariance matrices from data. In the simulations, the framework is evaluated for MIG detectors using both means and medians associated with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric, the LE metric, and the Bures--Wasserstein metric, on both simulated compound-Gaussian clutter and real IPIX sea clutter. In both cases, the HPDNet is trained solely on simulated data to assess its applicability to the study of real data. The results show a significant reduction of computational cost in testing, while maintaining detection performance and robustness.

title: A plug-in energy-balance freezing module for transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs
comment: 45 pages main text + 19 pages supplementary material
summary: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure. We develop a transformer-compatible module that embeds leaf energy-balance physics in freezing-probability forecasts: an energy-balance temperature reference and a learned residual predict leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a temperature-dependent probability cap. We mathematically prove conditional monotonicity and an alarm boundary, and test whether placing the same information in the output pathway or in attention yields different benefits. We evaluated 12 hourly leads at 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons, with and without leaf-sensor inputs. In the 2025-2026 hold-out season without these inputs, our time-token transformer (PET-E) achieved a lead-mean critical success index (CSI) of 0.516 versus 0.478 for fixed-configuration, joint-lead LightGBM, with significant gains at all 12 leads, and the fraction of alarms at observed leaf temperatures of at least 2 degrees C fell from 0.087 to 0.051 relative to the unmodified backbone. Across the hold-out and a retrospective 2024-2025 evaluation, the module reduced Brier scores and warm-surface alarm fractions in both the time-token transformer and iTransformer, with no significant CSI decrease at any lead. At held-out stations without static or leaf-sensor inputs, both module-equipped backbones exceeded LightGBM at all 12 leads (CSI 0.468 and 0.467 versus 0.437). In the time-token backbone, the temperature pathway reduced this alarm fraction in all four settings, whereas the attention prior increased CSI in three. These findings link an explicit temperature-dependent probability cap to improved forecasts and distinguish output-side from attention-based embedding.

title: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery
summary: Natural speech conveys meaning not only through words, but also through the prominence on a few words. Yet most text-to-speech (TTS) systems remain prominence-unaware, existing prominence-aware TTS require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate in isolation, disconnected from synthesis. This creates a fundamental gap no existing system can automatically discover where stress should be placed, realize it as natural-sounding prosody, and offer user control over emphasis placement, all within a single model. To circumvent this, we propose ProTTS, a unified framework where stress detection emerges from the TTS model itself and, in turn, guides it to synthesize more natural and controllable speech. We incorporate a clustering head into the variance adaptor of FastSpeech_2 that discovers word stress directly from aggregated prosodic features. The discovered stress then drives emphasis variance predictors that modify pitch, energy, and duration for stressed words. The framework is trained end-to-end: TTS reconstruction and clustering losses jointly shape a stress-discriminative feature space without requiring stress labels at any stage. At inference, the same architecture also supports user-controllable emphasis by accepting a custom stress mask. We evaluate ProTTS on ISLE (non-native), LibriTTS, VCTK (native training), and three evaluation benchmarks (Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, EmphAssess). Listeners prefer ProTTS over the baseline with a MOS of 3.96 vs. 3.12 and 83.5% preference rate. For stress detection, ProTTS achieves 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (German/Italian L2), outperforming unsupervised (0.70) and supervised (0.82) baselines, and 0.933 F1 in zero-shot transfer to Tatoeba.

title: Assessing Subgroup Heterogeneity in Carryover Effects: A Simulation Study and an Observational Alzheimer Disease Treatment-Transition Application
summary: Subgroup heterogeneity in carryover effects is not routinely evaluated in 2x2 crossover studies, and its inferential consequences remain insufficiently characterized. When the scientific question concerns subgroup-specific carryover, omission of the corresponding interaction causes the fitted model to target a collapsed population-average contrast rather than the subgroup difference of interest. We used simulation to evaluate the finite-sample bias, confidence-interval coverage, Type I error, and power of carryover-by-subgroup interaction inference under an independence-based analysis and REML-based MMRM analyses with CS and UN covariance specifications. Reduced mean models were included as population-average benchmarks. We also applied the models to observational Alzheimer disease treatment-transition sequences from NACC, where carryover was defined operationally as a model-based association with the preceding regimen rather than an identified pharmacologic persistence effect. Full models directly estimated subgroup-specific carryover heterogeneity, whereas reduced models estimated a collapsed carryover contrast that did not characterize this heterogeneity. Under the full mean model, point-estimate bias was small, whereas covariance misspecification affected empirical confidence-interval coverage and Type I error. Reliable inference on subgroup-specific carryover effects requires a mean model that explicitly represents the heterogeneity of interest and a covariance structure appropriate for the repeated-measures data. Failure to address either component can obscure subgroup differences or compromise statistical inference. These results provide practical guidance for evaluating heterogeneous carryover effects in crossover and treatment-transition studies.

title: Sparse Stabilization of Continuous-Time Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Efficient use of communication resources is crucial for stabilizing a networked control system. Employing \emph{sparse inputs} and event-triggered control are efficient ways to utilize communication resources in networked control systems. This work considers the problem of stabilizing a continuous-time linear dynamical system (LDS) using $s$-sparse inputs. For this purpose, we consider \emph{switched} linear feedback control, where we construct a finite number of feedback matrices with at most $s$ nonzero rows. Using switched systems theory, we show that there exists an $s$-sparse input for any sparsity level $s \geq 1$ that ensures stability when the continuous-time LDS is stabilizable. In addition, using our approach, we can compute the required feedback matrices with minimal overhead even if the sparsity budget $s$ varies over time. We also minimize the maximum Frobenius norm of the feedback matrices, yielding sparse inputs with reduced control energy. We show that an upper bound on the control energy required for stabilization using an $s$-sparse input is inversely proportional to $s^2$, while maintaining the same exponential stability rate. Finally, we combine the design of the \emph{sparse inputs} with the event-trigger rule to further reduce communication resource consumption. Our sparse and event-triggered control strategy ensures that any stabilizable continuous-time LDS can be stabilized using $s$-sparse inputs under both state feedback and output feedback, for any $s\geq 1$. We illustrate our theoretical results for the task of stabilizing a mass-spring system.

title: Causality and order restricted inference in the Aalen additive hasard model
summary:
We study a graphical model (DAG) with time to event as a response variable. We use the Aalen additive hazard model for modelling the effect on the response variable of covariates, combined with a multiple linear regression for earlier layers in a DAG. This enables modelling covariates affecting the event process both directly and indirectly. The indirect component effect is represented by a product $θ_1(t)β_2(t)$, where $θ_1(t)$ describes the effect of the independent covariate on the dependent covariate and $β_2(t)$ is the effect of the dependent covariate on the final time to response variable, in the additive hazard model. We estimate $β_2(t)$ by the order-restricted estimator recently introduced in Anevski and Merai (arXiv:2606.23882v2), thereby enabling disease models with early onset or late onset covariate effects. Combining our previously obtained results with the DAG allows for modelling early onset or late onset covariate effects together with direct and indirect covariate effects, which should be of particular interest for studying causality for complex diseases.
  We present a nonparametric plug-in estimator of the indirect effect. We derive the limit distribution of the plug-in estimator of the indirect component, and show that it has $n^{1/3}$ pointwise asymptotic rate and a limit distribution which is proportional to the Chernoff distribution.

title: Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled wireless-powered underground sensor networks (WPUSNs) allow underground devices (UDs) to harvest radio-frequency energy from a UAV via wireless energy transfer (WET) techniques, enabling sustainable Internet of underground things (IoUT) applications. This paper integrates rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA)-aided simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) into UAV-enabled WPUSNs to deliver information and energy to UDs. Within this framework, we investigate a max-min fairness problem that jointly optimizes the UAV transmit power, power allocation and message splitting, power-splitting ratios, and time allocation, aiming to maximize the minimum uplink throughput across UDs subject to per-UD downlink throughput requirements and a UAV energy-consumption constraint. To address this non-convex problem under dynamic underground environments, we develop an off-policy deep reinforcement learning approach based on the primal-dual truncated quantile critics (PD-TQC), where a TQC-based reward critic evaluates the fairness objective, cost critics estimate constraint costs, and an actor learns the resource-control policy with adaptive dual-variable updates. Simulations using in-situ soil volumetric water content measurements from a center-pivot irrigation farm demonstrate that PD-TQC achieves the highest annual average minimum uplink throughput compared with four benchmarks while satisfying the per-frame constraints in over 96% of the evaluated frames, and that this throughput advantage is preserved under different Rician factors, numbers of UDs, and downlink throughput thresholds.

title: Phase Transitions in Heavy-Tailed Mean Estimation under $\ell_p$ Norms
summary: We study the problem of estimating the mean of a random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ under $\ell_p$ norms, assuming only the existence of a covariance matrix. In the Euclidean norm, the sample mean is already optimal in expectation, and robust estimators are usually needed only to obtain high-probability tails. Our results show that this picture changes for $\ell_p$ norms with $p>2$: robustification is already necessary even for the expected risk. We prove that the minimax risk exhibits a sharp phase transition, controlled by the interaction between the sample size $n$, the dimension $d$, and the norm parameter $p$. In the large-sample regime, the classical Gaussian rate remains achievable. In the complementary regime, heavy-tailed distributions create a genuinely non-Gaussian obstruction. Furthermore we show that the simple estimator: coordinate-wise median of means whose number of buckets chosen according to the geometry of the loss, optimally tracks this phase transition in its expected risk minimax. We also show that natural projection-based median-of-means estimators for general norms, despite achieving the optimal confidence trade-off relative to the sample-mean benchmark of Lugosi and Mendelson (Probab. Theory Relat. Fields, 2019), can be polynomially suboptimal for $\ell_p$ norms even in the constant-probability regime.

title: Large Language Model-based Optimization for Wireless Communication: A Survey
summary: The growing complexity and dynamism of modern wireless communication frameworks have made real-time optimization essential for efficient resource allocation. Traditional optimization and machine-learning techniques often struggle with generalization, adaptability, stability, and scalability in heterogeneous, time-varying environments. Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools capable of reasoning over structured prompts and generating context-aware decisions in real time without domain-specific retraining. This survey provides a comprehensive review of LLM-driven optimization techniques applied to wireless communication problems such as power control, bandwidth allocation, task offloading, and intelligent surface configuration. We introduce a functional taxonomy of LLM-enabled wireless resource management strategies and analyze the prompt engineering methodologies employed in recent literature. Furthermore, we develop a generalized analytical framework that categorizes LLM-based optimization architectures, including direct solution generation, closed-loop optimization with external verifiers, and representation encoding within trainable neural pipelines. To demonstrate practical applicability, we present representative case studies on LLM-assisted beam prediction for millimeter-wave systems and adaptive wireless resource allocation. Finally, we discuss emerging hybrid AI approaches for wireless networks.

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Ordinal Functional Data with Application in Diabetes Intervention
summary: Traditional functional principal component analysis (FPCA) is typically designed for continuous functional observations. In this paper, we address the scenario where the outcome consists of repeated categorical data defined over a bounded interval. Our objective is to develop an FPCA methodology tailored specifically for ordinal functional data. Our approach leverages recent advancements in ordinal data modeling to estimate both the mean function and the eigenfunctions, while employing a computationally efficient method for predicting the scores. The performance of the proposed methodology is evaluated numerically in simulation and data application on diabetes intervention.

title: Wideband Hybrid Beamforming via Programmable Unitary Mixer--TTD RF Networks
summary: This paper proposes a wideband hybrid beamforming architecture whose analog front-end consists of fixed unitary mixers interlaced with programmable diagonal phase-shift/true-time-delay (TTD) layers. Under ideal passive-component assumptions, the analog beamformer is semi-unitary on every OFDM subcarrier, so the injected RF-chain power reaches the antenna ports without analog-network loss. We design the phase shifts and delays of the programmable diagonal phase-shift/TTD layers for OFDM sum-rate maximization. Numerical results show that increasing mixer--TTD depth improves the sum rate under ideal component assumptions and a common injected RF-power budget. With component losses included, a shallow design retains an advantage over the evaluated hybrid baselines at low-to-moderate powers, motivating deeper implementations with low accumulated loss.

title: Integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders for Disentangled Representation Learning
summary: We introduce LBM-VAE, a novel framework that integrates Latent Block Models (LBMs) into Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to jointly cluster observations and latent dimensions. Beyond its clustering capabilities, LBM-VAE provides a block-structured latent representation that naturally supports disentangled representation learning. In contrast to conventional approaches that associate each factor of variation with an individual latent dimension, our framework allows factors of variation to be encoded across groups of latent dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate the promising clustering performance of LBM-VAE, while achieving competitive results in disentangled representation learning. LBM-VAE highlights the potential of combining co-clustering and variational inference to learn structured and interpretable latent representations.

title: Equal Dose, Different Coverage:Tracing Rate and Duration in Image Editing
summary: Benchmarks for scientific image editing test whether a model draws the outcome of a described process, leaving open which representations carry its errors and whether correcting them yields the right quantity. We study this question with an airbrush of fixed deposition profile, under which exchanging rate and duration preserves the dose and should preserve the endpoint, yet changes the edited coverage. Matched-norm activation patches across text positions and denoising stages show that, in distilled FLUX with Chinese prompts, representations at unchanged text positions (context) carry this discrepancy: early context transfers 3.51 of the 3.98 percentage-point (pp) signed route difference, against 0.09 pp for equal-norm updates at the two changed digits. Early image latents transmit native (unpatched) route differences across two FLUX configurations and OmniGen, while text-position effects depend on configuration. The trace predicts an intervention: share early context between routes while each retains its own digits. On independent English layouts, this reduces the distilled-FLUX absolute route gap from 1.13 to 0.60 pp, outperforms early digit sharing, and improves agreement more than in base FLUX under directly paired tests. Calibrated evaluation, which prescribes an area for each dose, separates this gain from accuracy: sharing the full prompt encoding produces identical route images with target errors of 8-16 pp, and stating the target percentage directly retains a compressed area response. Localization predicts a consistency gain on new layouts, and calibration measures the quantity error that agreement leaves unresolved.

title: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
summary: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. In the Manifold-Index Model, the mean response is $F=f\circΠ_{\mathcal{M}}$, where $Π_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the nearest-point projection onto $\mathcal{M}$ and $f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^p$ is a possibly non-injective link function. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. Numerical experiments on curves with non-monotone links and surfaces with vector-valued responses compare observed convergence rates with the theoretical bounds; a Langevin dynamics example tests prediction of hitting probabilities under an approximate manifold-index model.

title: Physics-Informed Fractional Load Forecasting With Memory-Aware Break Detection for Reserve Scheduling
summary: Day-ahead load forecasts set balancing reserves, including the energy a pumped-storage plant holds against forecast errors. Both depend on three effects that are usually modeled separately, namely the thermal inertia of buildings, which makes load lag temperature, structural breaks, which shift demand, and the long memory of forecast errors, which keeps them from cancelling out. We prove that averaging building responses over Cole-Cole distributed time constants yields a fractional temperature kernel with nonnegative weights exactly when its order is at most one. A Bayesian information criterion that ignores long memory selects spurious breaks with probability tending to one, so breaks and memory are estimated jointly, and an online break detector keeps its false-alarm rate below any prescribed level. Long memory also makes the required storage energy grow faster than the square root of the horizon, so a second-order cone program schedules reserves from the joint distribution of hourly errors. On New England and Mid-Atlantic data including the 2020 pandemic, the proposed framework improves on the best of ten benchmarks by 15.7% and 10.3% in mean absolute percentage error. Its reserves breach the storage energy limit on 4.1% and 8.5% of days, against 36.7% and 57.5% with error correlations ignored.

title: Medicaid Quality Disparities: Domain-Specific Performance Analysis and Approaches for State-Level Improvement
summary: Medicaid covers nearly 78 million people, yet care quality varies across states, programs, and clinical domains. Using the 2024 CMS Child and Adult Core Sets (9,781 usable state-measure observations from 11,100 records), this study combined descriptive statistics, benchmark-gap analysis, correlation, and OLS regression to find where shortfalls cluster. Disparities were strongly domain-specific. Maternal and Perinatal Health scored lowest (28.0%), followed by Dental and Oral Health (38.5%) and Behavioral Health (44.4%), while Long-Term Services and Supports (82.8%) and Experience of Care (67.8%) scored highest. State performance correlated strongly with national benchmarks (r = 0.77, approximately), so rates should be read against each measure's benchmark. Domain was the strongest predictor, and the model explained 31.2% of variance. Because of heteroscedasticity and influential observations from mixing bounded and utilization measures, estimates are descriptive. Quality improvement should be targeted by domain, prioritizing maternal health, behavioral health network adequacy, and dental provider participation.

title: The Grid's Own Language: A Common Information Model Layer for LLM Grid Assistants
summary: Assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are entering power system operation. Current designs delegate computations to validated solvers, but the agent still infers the type, role and state of each element from its name and tool-specific formats, and errors propagate to every study. The Common Information Model (CIM), the IEC standard in which operators already exchange network models, defines unambiguously what each element is and how it connects. We propose a CIM layer for LLM grid assistants and implement it in CONDUCTOR, an open-source assistant. Both the agent and its power-system studies read the layer. It labels the provenance of each fact (stated in the data, suggested only by a name, or inferred from topology), loads operators' CGMES models directly, and builds in $\leq$1\,s on the 9,241-bus PEGASE network. Deterministic checks compare every answer with solver results and the layer. On 37 tasks about the CIGRE medium-voltage and IEEE 30-bus networks, the agent gets right 97\,\% of the graded facts with the layer, such as a unit's energy source or a switch's normal state, against 55\,\% without it. We argue that a CIM layer should be a default component of grid assistants.

title: Maximum Scores and Treatment Feedback in Regression Discontinuity Designs
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Code and replication-level results in ancillary files
summary: Hospitals use repeated risk scores to decide when to send an alert. Some evaluations summarize these scores by their maximum and use the maximum as the running variable in a regression discontinuity (RD) design. The maximum shows correctly whether a patient was ever alerted. However, it can include scores recorded after an earlier alert has already changed care. In this paper, we study what the maximum-score RD estimates when an earlier intervention changes a later score. We use a two-assessment model and derive a formula that splits the RD contrast into the causal effect and a composition term. When feedback moves scores in one direction, the composition term equals the relative jump in the density of the maximum at the cutoff times a prognostic contrast. Therefore, an exactly continuous density means no bias, and the population density jump bounds the bias. Valid inference on the jump turns this into a confidence bound under a stated sensitivity assumption. Within this model, bias behind a continuous density requires feedback in both directions. For this case, we bound bias by total boundary movement and construct conservative confidence sets for binary outcomes under explicit sensitivity and smoothness assumptions. We give closed forms for independent uniform scores and for correlated Gaussian scores. In one example, a true risk reduction of four percentage points appears as a one-point increase. Simulations confirm the formulas. Narrower bandwidths, robust bias correction, and machine-learning covariate adjustment do not remove the bias. A fuzzy RD on the first score recovers the causal effect when early and late treatment have the same effect. Our results concern how the running variable is built. We do not assess any published clinical study.

title: Clinician Assessment of Laryngeal Disease with Auditory AI before Laryngoscopy: A Paired Reader Study
summary:
Background: Before laryngoscopy, clinicians assess the likely cause of hoarseness and whether to suspect a precancerous or malignant lesion. Whether voice-based artificial intelligence (AI) supports pre-laryngoscopic categorization is unknown.
  Methods: We developed an auditory large language model that generates a patient-level assessment card (provisional category, voice-quality ratings, and rationale) and a prespecified malignancy alert from voice recordings, patient information, and acoustic measures obtained before laryngoscopy at one center. We evaluated both in a held-out test set and a later cohort. In a sequential reader study, 32 otolaryngology clinicians categorized held-out cases without AI and, 1 to 2 weeks later, reviewed their initial categories with the card (without the alert).
  Results: Across 800 paired assessments, reader accuracy was 49.8% before and 56.8% after review (difference, 7.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.7 to 13.5; P < 0.001); 99 categories changed from incorrect to correct and 43 from correct to incorrect (ratio, 2.30; 95% CI, 1.22 to 5.31). Accuracy rose 14.7 points when the model was correct and fell 8.7 when incorrect. Provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation. The malignancy alert flagged 85.7% and 86.8% of precancerous or malignant lesions. Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions increased from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review (difference, 21.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.3 to 42.0).
  Conclusions: In this single-center study, clinicians' pre-laryngoscopic categorization accuracy was higher after reviewing the AI assessment card, although the sequential design cannot fully separate AI assistance from reassessment; gains depended on model correctness without clearly selective adoption. Randomized and external evaluations, including of the malignancy alert, are needed.

title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
summary: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. Most models in use do not update by exact conditioning and are not guaranteed to be coherent, which can lead to worse decisions. Yet there is currently no general way to measure incoherence or to tell when it matters. We develop tools to measure incoherence and characterise when it affects decisions. We introduce the incoherence ratio, an MMD-based measure of how far any updating procedure departs from coherence, computed only from the procedure's own predictions and updates, and accompany it with an anytime-valid test of coherence. In Bayesian experimental design, acquisition objectives that are equivalent for coherent models choose different data under every approximate model we study, and the incoherence ratio tracks how far incoherence distorts them. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.

title: SWAN-Rx: Efficient and Bandwidth-Scalable Neural Reception for MIMO-OFDM
comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: We present a Scalable Windowed Axial-attention Neural Receiver (SWAN-Rx) for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. The receiver improves reception accuracy and reduces forward-pass computation while supporting frozen-weight reuse across bandwidth allocations and channel conditions. It combines a common resource-element representation of received observations and pilot context with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention. Shared parameters and relative positional information permit soft detection across allocation lengths without inference-time parameter updates. At fixed subcarrier spacing, model configuration, and symbol count, bounded frequency neighborhoods give linear growth of forward-pass computation with bandwidth. Evaluations compatible with the 5G New Radio physical layer reuse weights trained on four physical resource blocks (PRBs) at up to 273 PRBs and on unseen channels. At the training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx achieves lower pre- and post-decoding bit error rates than the implemented three-step neural receiver (NRX) and DeepRx-MIMO baselines, with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, respectively. The same weights achieve lower pre-decoding error rates than these baselines throughout the evaluated bandwidth-extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests, with an estimated 0.4-0.9 dB signal-to-noise ratio reduction relative to NRX at a pre-decoding error rate of $10^{-2}$ in the 16-PRB tests.

title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
summary: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

title: Density-First Design of Anti-Jamming Sparse Spreading Codes for NB-IoT
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Extended version of a paper to appear in Proc. IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM), Washington, DC, Oct. 2026. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications
summary: As narrowband Internet of Things (NB-IoT) systems continue to be deployed in increasingly heterogeneous and demanding wireless environments, including those characterized by interference, high mobility, and potentially hostile conditions, enhancing the resilience of the physical-layer waveform has become an important and timely design consideration. Motivated by this need, the present paper introduces a density-first framework for the design of anti-jamming sparse spreading codes in NB-IoT systems. Building on this framework, we propose a generalized method for constructing sparse codes that decouples column density from the conventional Alamouti-paired structure, thereby enabling both disjoint-support and deterministic code designs. In addition, we develop a generative machine-learning approach based on a variational autoencoder for synthesizing jamming-robust sparse spreading codes. To evaluate the performance of sparse spreading under conditions of additive white Gaussian noise, fading, and pulse jamming, we present a bit-error-rate (BER) analysis framework. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations, conducted across a wide range of density, channel, and jamming conditions, show that the performance of sparse spreading codes is determined primarily by column density rather than by optimization of code coefficients. In particular, highly sparse codes with disjoint support offer the greatest robustness to jamming while avoiding the unfavorable intermediate-density regime. Relative to the prior-art Alamouti-paired low-density spreading code, the recommended uniform-density design reduces pulse-jamming BER by roughly 5 times; a deterministic Lempel-Costas construction attains the empirical optimum in closed form, while the variational-autoencoder generator yields a further 45% improvement over the best algebraic design.

title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
summary: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Lookup Table Demappers for Amplitude Phase-Shift Keying over Nonlinear Satellite Links
summary: Next-generation high-throughput satellites increasingly demodulate and decode on board, so the per-symbol cost of the receiver constrains payload power and throughput. Soft demappers for nonlinear satellite links must therefore produce accurate bit log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) at low cost. We introduce a KAN-LUT demapper, a two-layer Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN) whose learned univariate edge functions are stored as 128-entry lookup tables (LUTs), so that inference needs only table reads, linear interpolation, and additions. We bound the LLR error introduced by the tables and evaluate the demapper on amplitude phase-shift keying (APSK) links with low-density parity-check (LDPC) coding and a nonlinear traveling-wave-tube amplifier. For 16-, 32-, and 64-APSK, KAN-LUT stays within 0.2 dB of a per-cluster Gaussian log-MAP (LogMAP-CG) demapper, while its cost relative to LogMAP-CG falls from 87% to 27% as the order grows. It matches or slightly exceeds multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) at about one fifth of their cost, remains competitive under operating-point mismatch, and needs only tens of kilobytes of tables. KAN-LUT is therefore a low-cost candidate demapper for regenerative payloads.

title: Decorrelation Before Variable Selection: Left and Right Transforms and Their Trade-Off
summary: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients. Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true ones come first; decorrelation preserving coefficients and noise loses information.

title: Consensus-based Economic Dispatch for Self-organized Local Energy Communities
summary: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) is transforming traditional distribution networks into dynamic, decentralized systems, creating a pressing need for scalable, autonomous coordination mechanisms that do not rely on centralized control or full system observability. In particular, local energy communities need to self-organize and coordinate energy schedules while respecting network constraints, especially voltage limits, despite lacking detailed knowledge of the distribution grid's topology and parameters. Existing distributed optimization approaches either neglect such physical constraints or assume perfect knowledge of the network model. This paper addresses the Voltage-Constrained Economic Dispatch (VCED) problem in a fully decentralized, consensus-based manner, without any coordinating entity. We use sparse-group LASSO regression to learn a linear surrogate of nodal voltages from local power and voltage measurements alone. The surrogate serves a dual purpose: it enters each agent's local problem as a voltage penalty and induces the communication graph over which the agents reach consensus. We provide a theoretical bound on the optimality loss caused by the surrogate voltage estimator inaccuracy. Our numerical results, on an IEEE-33 network, show that the scheme reduces the share of bus-timesteps voltage violations from 30\% to below 3\%, while staying within 1\% of a centralized benchmark computed with full network knowledge. We further quantify how the sparsity of the communication graph affects both the optimality gap and the residual violations.

title: False Discovery Rate Control in Ordered Sequential Testing: Rejection-Count and Fallback Procedures
comment: 47 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Includes proofs in appendices
summary: We study false discovery rate (FDR) control for a fixed family of hypotheses tested sequentially in a prespecified order. Each decision uses only the current and preceding $p$-values, is not subsequently revised, and permits continued testing after non-rejections. We distinguish generalized fixed-sequence procedures based on preceding rejection counts from fallback-type procedures that additionally use recursively transferred testing levels. For rejection-count procedures, we study a position-dependent calibration under independence and a linear rule calibrated through null marginal distribution functions under positive left-tail dependence under the null. We clarify their connections to existing fixed-sequence and online FDR methods. The fallback construction combines the total number of preceding discoveries with level transfer along consecutive rejections, allowing thresholds to reflect the arrangement of earlier outcomes. We establish its FDR control under history-based positive regression dependence and, with a position-specific correction, under arbitrary dependence. For all four constructions, the guarantees extend to every deterministic testing time within the planned horizon. Gaussian simulations assess the effects of signal placement, dependence, and allocation weights. They demonstrate power gains over selected benchmarks while identifying the conservativeness of the arbitrary-dependence correction.

title: A Geometric Observer for Visual-Inertial Odometry using Optical-Flow Constraints
summary: This paper presents a geometric observer for monocular visual-inertial odometry driven by individual optical-flow constraints. For each tracked point, the bearing and its rotationally compensated derivative give a depth-free homogeneous constraint on the body-frame velocity. These constraints enter the innovation of an observer on the gravity-augmented group $\mathbb{SE}_3(3)$ through a Riccati gain, without estimating depths or reconstructing the direction of motion. The auxiliary gravity state makes the six-dimensional body-frame velocity-gravity error dynamics independent of the attitude correction, and their uniform observability is shown to be equivalent to persistent excitation of a matrix formed from the inertial bearings and their derivatives. Under this condition, the body-frame velocity and gravity errors converge globally and uniformly exponentially, and a gravity-based attitude correction renders the combined velocity, gravity, and reduced-attitude error almost globally asymptotically stable and locally uniformly exponentially stable. Simulations illustrate the excitation condition, recovery from initial errors, and sensitivity to perturbed measurements.

title: Decomposition Bounds for MCMC with Mixture Targets: Multimodality and Heavy-Tailedness
summary: We establish quantitative mixing-time bounds for Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms targeting multimodal and heavy-tailed mixtures. The dynamics of a Markov chain are decomposed into local and global levels, and possibly weak Poincaré inequalities at both levels are combined to form convergence bounds. We apply this framework to location and scale mixtures of strongly log-concave distributions, obtaining explicit convergence bounds for random-walk Metropolis, proximal, and random-scan Gibbs samplers. For location mixtures connected along a finite path, the bounds depend polynomially on the number of components and exponentially on neighboring separation, remaining informative as the overall diameter grows. For scale mixtures, we relate the global dynamics of the chain to the isoperimetry of the log-scale mixing distribution, and illustrate the effect of heavy-tailed targets by examining inverse-gamma mixing distributions.

title: Locational Marginal Pricing of Compute: Co-optimizing Compute and Energy for Transparent Data Center Flexibility
summary: Demand from data centers and AI compute is growing rapidly and is increasing stress on the power grid. This load could be flexible through user adjustments and provide relief during energy scarcity events, yet today its flexibility is provided through utility call-ups or system-operator load shedding, and is invisible to the users whose workloads are being curtailed. In this work, we propose to quantify and couple the prices of compute and energy in a single optimization problem. The resulting compute price reflects the marginal cost of the binding constraints and decomposes into components indicating which grid, power, hardware, or service requirement causes a price surge. The economic interpretation updates the price with real-time conditions and gives users a signal for potential flexibility provision. The co-optimization ultimately connects compute and energy markets while providing a signal for relief of stress on both the grid and the compute resources.

title: Limit theorems and bias correction for the initial-noise-adjusted SIML estimator
summary: We propose a sine-based modification of the separating information maximum likelihood (SIML) estimator for integrated volatility and covariance under equidistant sampling with microstructure noise. The estimator allows for nonzero initial observation noise. We establish consistency under moment assumptions and asymptotic normality under first-order Malliavin regularity of the diffusion coefficients. We also construct a feasible noise-bias correction using an estimator of the unknown noise covariance. This correction permits wider spectral bandwidths for consistency and stable asymptotic normality.

title: Spatial phase coherence and its applications to masking and adaptive neighborhood sizing in multitemporal InSAR
summary: We examine spatial phase coherence (SPC), a measure of the correlation between the wrapped phase time series of two pixels in a stack of single-look synthetic aperture radar acquisitions. A pixel and its adjacent neighbors share speckle through the point spread function, so that decorrelation alone does not lower their SPC below a floor. We find that masking pixels whose mean SPC to their eight neighbors is well below that floor, as in parts of layover and shadow areas, is an inexpensive complement to geometry-derived layover and shadow masks. For distributed scatterer pixels, averaging SPC over a fixed set of neighbors that share no speckle yields a proxy for the local coherence, the phase coherence indicator (PCI), that is available before the selection of statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs). In phase estimation, averaging more pixels reduces noise but may also increase the bias in heterogeneous areas. To relax this trade-off, we propose to enhance SHP selection algorithms by scaling the search window size according to the PCI and truncating the set of selected pixels where a smaller nested set agrees clearly better with the phases at the center. In simulations of a TerraSAR-X and a Sentinel-1 stack with 44 and 79 acquisitions, we apply this adaptive neighborhood sizing (ANS) to established amplitude- and covariance-based SHP selection algorithms with thresholds that adapt to the PCI. Without ANS, the largest tested search window size has 13 to 29 % more phase linking error than the best of the tested sizes. With ANS, the largest window has the lowest error of the tested sizes, 11 % lower than that of the same selection at its best tested size without ANS. On a real TerraSAR-X stack, the mask based on SPC flags pixels in building shadows that a terrain model misses. On real Sentinel-1 stacks, ANS preserves dense fringes on a slowly deforming slope and in part on a fast landslide.

title: multiCAsp: Spatially Informed Canonical Association Analysis of Multi-Omic Data
summary: Simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers at spatially resolved locations creates opportunities to identify shared cross-modal biological variation in its tissue context. We present multiCAsp (multi-omic Canonical Association informed by spatial graph), a probabilistic latent-factor model for integrating $M \geq 2$ spatially resolved omic modalities. It incorporates spatial dependence through a graph-Laplacian prior on shared latent factors and uses an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate factor scores and modality-specific feature loadings. Because the prior is defined on a neighborhood graph rather than on Euclidean distances, it accommodates irregular tissue geometries and extends naturally to multiple tissue sections. Simulations show that multiCAsp consistently achieves higher mean latent subspace and loading recovery than alternative methods across varying sample sizes, feature dimensions, and noise levels, with the largest gains under high noise. Compared with an existing Gaussian process-based spatial factor model, it is also less sensitive to how the spatial coordinates are represented, produces spatially smoother factors, and has lower computational cost. Applied to metabolomic-proteomic data from macaque cortex and gene-protein data from human renal carcinoma, multiCAsp recovers spatially coherent multi-omic factors with interpretable biological signatures. In the macaque data, transferred factors retain broad spatial patterns across animals and support cross-modal prediction of protein abundances from metabolomic measurements.

title: Kernel-Guided Learning of Lifted Sparse Polynomial Models of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
summary: Polynomial models of dynamical systems enable constructive analysis via sum-of-squares programming. Yet, many physical systems involve non-polynomial nonlinearities which for certain classes of systems may be inferred from the underlying physics even when the exact dynamics are unknown. We show that fitting lifted polynomial models directly to lifted data is problematic, since the exact lifting constraints render the lifted derivatives linearly dependent. Instead, we learn the dynamics in the extended state, i.e., the state together with the known nonlinearities, and obtain the dynamics of the nonlinearities via the exact lifting relations. To avoid the combinatorially large libraries that sparse regression requires when the polynomial degrees are unknown, we propose KINDy, which selects the degree of each component by kernel ridge regression before applying sparse regression to the correspondingly reduced library. We prove that, for sufficiently small noise and regularization, provided the data satisfy a rank condition, the selected degree never underestimates the true degree. On the cart-pole system, KINDy recovers the true degrees at low noise levels and achieves speedups of up to 8.5 over sparse regression on the full library, while in almost all cases yielding models that are at least as sparse and have lower or equal test errors.

title: Two-Stage Staffing with Random Arrival Rate: A Simulation Optimization Approach
summary: In service systems, the arrival rate in the same time period and day of the week exhibits randomness, yet can be more accurately estimated or forecast right before that period, which motivates a two-stage staffing scheme with advance base staffing and pre-shift surge staffing. Existing approaches usually impose strong assumptions on the arrival process and service systems' operational logic and other further approximations (i.e., stylized models) to derive explicit staffing policies. This paper proposes a simulation optimization approach (SOA) for more general arrival processes and service systems by effectively addressing some intertwined challenges. By recasting the original formulation into computationally tractable structures and designing an efficient coordinate-search algorithm, it constructs a two-stage staffing lookup table offline, which allows managers to make real-time surge staffing decisions without any further simulation. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed SOA has significantly better staffing performance and substantially broader applicability compared to existing approaches. Even under the stylized models, the cost savings delivered by our SOA compared with existing approaches range from the low tens to several tens of percent, depending on different problem parameters; the advantage further amplifies when the actual problem deviates from the stylized models. In a nurse-staffing case study grounded in real-world data, the proposed SOA delivers approximately 8% to 13% cost savings over a state-of-the-art benchmark.

title: Cross-Subject Priors for Maximum a Posteriori Estimation of Latent Structure Influence Models in Motor-Imagery EEG With Few Trials
summary: Coupled hidden Markov models such as the latent structure influence model (LSIM) describe how the sensorimotor rhythms of the two hemispheres evolve and interact during motor imagery, but subject-specific maximum likelihood (ML) estimates are unstable when few trials are available. This paper derives a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator for the LSIM whose conjugate prior equals the expected statistics of $λ$ pseudo-trials from a population model fitted to other subjects. The M-step remains in closed form, expectation maximization keeps its monotone ascent, and ML ($λ=0$) and the population model ($λ\to\infty$) are limiting cases. The prior strength was selected on 35 subjects of the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset and applied unchanged to 70 held-out subjects and to BCI Competition IV-2a. With $λ=1$ the held-out log-likelihood exceeded that of ML in 61 of 70 subjects (Holm-adjusted $p=9.1\times10^{-8}$) and in all 70 subjects with five training trials per class. A prior learned only from the PhysioNet data improved the held-out likelihood of all nine BCI IV-2a subjects at five trials per class and reduced the error of the joint transition matrix by 61%. Decoding accuracy did not improve ($p=0.17$). Cross-subject priors therefore stabilize few-trial dynamic models of motor-imagery EEG, but they do not improve decoding, which in these data relies mainly on structure shared across subjects.

title: Semiparametric regression with stagewise empirical risk minimization
summary: Maintaining both interpretability and accuracy remains a fundamental challenge in regression analysis. This paper addresses these two objectives through a semiparametric approach that combines a parametric crude guess with its nonparametric adjustment. In particular, the nonparametric adjustment is implemented via a machine learning technique called ``stagewise empirical risk minimization algorithm.'' Once a set (dictionary) of functions (words) is prepared, this algorithm constructs a convex combination of words selected iteratively from the dictionary. This selection is based on the empirical risk derived from the Bregman divergence, which enables the proposed estimators to be applied in broad settings, including generalized linear models. This paper examines these proposed semiparametric estimators theoretically and numerically. In the theoretical study, we derive a non-asymptotic error bound for the estimators constructed from a general data-dependent dictionary. Among the concrete dictionaries proposed in this paper, some can be utilized to correct variable selection in LASSO-based parametric regression, which is investigated in the numerical study. Moreover, simulation studies investigate practical performance of the proposed estimators, while real data applications further confirm their predictive performance. These studies indicate that the proposed semiparametric estimators can address the above challenge in several settings.

title: Streaming across viewing conditions - The effect of viewing distance and display luminance on video quality
summary: The visibility of streamed video distortions is affected by the user's display and viewing conditions, such as their display's luminance or the viewing distance. Distortions become less visible at lower luminance levels or farther viewing distances. However, most image and video quality metrics assume fixed optimal display and viewing conditions, making them insensitive to the viewing conditions. In this work, we demonstrate how existing metrics can be adapted to account for both factors and compare such an adaptation with the metrics that natively model viewing conditions. First, we collected a new video quality dataset, HDR-VDC, which contains streaming distortions in 4K HDR videos. The dataset consists of 12 4K and 4 FHD HDR source video content, each distorted with AV1 encoding and Lanczos upscaling from a lower resolution. The quality loss due to the distortions was measured at two viewing distances, corresponding to 60 and 120 pixels per visual degree, and two display mean luminance levels, varying by a factor of 8 in terms of luminance. Next, we developed a pre-processing framework that lets us adapt many quality metrics so that they can evaluate content across the viewing distances and luminance levels. The framework employs a display model and perceptually uniform encoding, PU21, to account for the effect of display luminance, and perspective projection scaling (PPS) to account for the effect of viewing distance. We used the framework to compare the performance of 35 state-of-the-art metrics. This allowed us to identify a selection of existing quality metrics that can be effectively adapted to account for the viewing conditions.

title: Bayesian variable selection via collapsed importance-weighted variational inference over discrete model spaces
summary: Bayesian variable selection under spike-and-slab priors provides interpretable posterior inclusion probabilities for individual predictors, but exploring large discrete model spaces using conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be computationally challenging. We develop a collapsed importance-weighted variational framework for Gaussian linear regression. The framework analytically integrates out the remaining model parameters and directly approximates the posterior over binary inclusion indicators using a factorised Bernoulli distribution. To improve posterior inclusion probability estimation while retaining the computational simplicity of the factorised variational family, we replace the conventional evidence lower bound with a tighter variational Rényi importance-weighted lower bound. We establish a finite-sample upper bound on posterior inclusion probability approximation errors and show that, under suitable conditions, the optimised variational inclusion probabilities converge to their exact posterior counterparts as the number of importance samples increases and the Rényi parameter decreases appropriately. We further establish that analytical marginalisation tightens the variational objective and the corresponding inclusion probability error bound, while reducing importance-weight variance and improving the asymptotic efficiency of importance-sampling post-processing. To address the challenges of estimating gradients with respect to the variational parameters when the inclusion indicators are discrete, we leverage recent advances in variance-reduced score-function estimators, together with an annealing strategy to stabilise optimisation. Simulation experiments and empirical applications demonstrate improvements in posterior inclusion probability estimation relative to standard variational inference and two existing variational approaches.

title: VoxMel TTS Technical Report
summary: Continuous autoregressive TTS relies on an acoustic target that enables stable next-latent modeling while preserving fine-grained acoustic details. While existing approaches employ learned compressed representations (e.g., continuous VAE latents) to render prediction tractable, they rely on complex neural encoders that often cap generation fidelity. Conversely, training-free targets like mel-spectrograms eliminate encoder overhead, yet their potential for autoregressive generation remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose VoxMel, a tokenizer-free framework for autoregressive TTS that makes stable mel modeling tractable through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. The transform first decomposes each mel spectrogram along frequency into local averages and a frequency residual, then splits the averaged component along time into Coarse-Mel and a temporal residual. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively generates Coarse-Mel. Non-autoregressive residual tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel, followed by the frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Neither residual is fed back into the autoregressive history. Trained on 100K hours of Emilia, the supervised 0.6B model obtains 1.51\% WER and 0.738 speaker similarity (SIM) on test-en, and 1.29\% CER and 0.755 SIM on test-zh. GRPO improves these results to 1.15\% WER / 0.753 SIM and 1.17\% CER / 0.776 SIM, respectively. We also distill the guided flow head into two- and four-step students, requiring 2 or 4 head evaluations per coarse frame. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER.

title: Sharp Local Entropy Bounds in the Wasserstein Space
summary: Fréchet regression extends regression analysis to metric space-valued responses such as probability distributions. Its asymptotic theory often relies on local entropy conditions, which control the complexity of small balls in the response space. A commonly used condition requires the associated local entropy integral to remain bounded as the balls shrink, but this requirement can fail when the response space is infinite-dimensional. We determine the exact rate at which this integral diverges in the Wasserstein space of probability distributions supported on a compact interval. Specifically, for a broad class of ball centers, we establish matching upper and lower bounds for the local covering entropy and show that the local entropy integral grows at the rate of the reciprocal square root of the ball radius. This rate persists when the response space is restricted to a large class of continuous distributions. The same rate holds for uniform local entropy integrals, with the supremum taken over ball centers. These results quantify the local complexity of the Wasserstein space and provide sharp benchmarks for entropy assumptions in statistical problems with distribution-valued responses.

title: Continuous-Time Stochastic Contraction Induced by Common White Noise
summary: This paper studies contraction properties of stochastic dynamical systems governed by Itô stochastic differential equations. We consider two trajectories driven by a common noise process and measure their separation using Finsler distances, which encompass Riemannian and norm-induced distances. Two notions of contraction are then investigated: $L^p$-contraction, defined by exponential decay of the $L^p$-norm (or the $p$-th moment) of the distance, and almost sure contraction, defined by exponential decay of the distance along almost every sample path. Each notion is characterized by a differential condition that is necessary and sufficient for contraction under mild hypotheses. Relations between contraction notions and an associated incremental input-to-state stability result are also established. As an illustration, we apply the established theory to analyze noise-induced synchronization and quantify its robustness with respect to parameter perturbations.

title: A conic optimization framework for shape-constrained functional regression analysis
summary: Standard regression methods do not always guarantee that the estimated model reflects prior knowledge about how predictors relate to the response, which motivates constrained regression. When the effects to be estimated are smooth nonlinear functions, a natural family of constraints is that of shape constraints, such as sign, monotonicity, or curvature, which encode qualitative properties that these functions are often expected to satisfy. While shape-constrained estimation of smooth functions is well established in classical regression with scalar covariates and response, its extension to functional regression, where the coefficients are themselves functions, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose the functional shape-constrained conic P-spline estimator (FunSCOPE), a unified framework for shape-constrained functional linear regression that covers scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and function-on-function models, and in which any combination of the shapes above can be imposed on the functional regression coefficient. Building on a P-spline approach, the desired shapes are expressed as conditions on the scalar regression coefficients, which leads to an estimation problem formulated as a conic optimization problem. For univariate coefficients, as in scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and a particular case of the function-on-function regression, the concurrent case, these conditions are both necessary and sufficient, in contrast to existing approaches, which provide only sufficient conditions; for bivariate coefficients, as in general function-on-function models, they are neither necessary nor sufficient. Numerical experiments show that FunSCOPE outperforms competing methods in terms of estimation error and computational time.

title: Three-Dimensional Impact Angle Control Guidance Law with Field-of-View Constraint
summary: This paper presents a novel impact angle control guidance law to address the challenge of achieving any desired impact angle while satisfying the seeker's Field Of View (FOV) limit and maintaining acceleration continuity. The guidance problem is decomposed into two two-dimensional (2D) engagement planes. In the first plane, a pure proportional navigation guidance (PNG) law is employed toward a virtual target to align the missile velocity vector with the line-of-sight (LOS) to the target. In the second plane, a two-stage time-varying biased PNG (TVBPN) strategy is utilized to accurately shape the trajectory and achieve the desired terminal impact angle while maintaining compliance with FOV limitations. The position of the virtual target point ensures a smooth and continuous lateral acceleration at the transition between the first and second stages. The effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed law were validated through numerical simulations.

title: Optimal Importance Sampling Densities for Estimating Several Expectations at Once
summary: Simulation studies often estimate several quantities from a single sample, and the best importance sampling density depends on how the errors on these quantities are combined. We characterise the optimal auxiliary density for a general error criterion. We show that it is the nominal density reweighted by a weighted length of the vector of estimated functions, where the weights are set by the error criterion, or by the curvature of the loss when the criterion comes from a loss on the errors. We also provide a lower bound on the best achievable error. The optimal density is explicit for smooth losses, including the usual losses on covariance matrices. We also derive allocation laws for the cells of a histogram and characterise the minimax density for the probabilities of several events. When there is no closed form, we show how to compute the optimal density numerically.

title: ANNA: Attention-Free Neural Neighborhood Aggregation for Channel Estimation on Regenerative NTN Payloads
summary: Accurate deep learning (DL)-based channel estimation (CE) for non-terrestrial network (NTN) uplinks must meet the processing, power, and latency constraints of regenerative payloads.
